item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers are going to the World Series for the second time in franchise history and the first time as a National League team (the Brewers were still in the American League when they went to the World Series in 1982). This also means the Los Angeles Dodgers have been eliminated, and their shot at becoming baseball's first threepeat champion since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees ended on Thursday night. The Brewers have swept the Dodgers in four games in the NLCS, doing so one year after the Dodgers swept them in the 2025 NLCS.
Who is to blame for the Dodgers going four-and-out in the NLCS? There's plenty of blame to go around, so let's assign it, shall we?
1. The Brewers
Milwaukee continues to be baseball's best team
We have to start here. The Dodgers got swept in the NLCS because the Brewers outplayed them in every phase of the game. The Brewers got better starting pitching. Their bullpen was better. Their defense and baserunning were better. Their offense was better at both stringing together hits to build a rally and launching the ball out of the park. Pat Murphy out-managed Dave Roberts as well. You name it, and the Brewers did it better than the Dodgers this series.
"It's a pretty simple answer," Dodgers infielder Max Muncy said after Game 3. "We're playing like shit. They're playing great."
As much as we want to (and will) blame various Dodgers for the sweep, the single biggest reason they got swept is that the Brewers were simply the better team. They were the better team in the regular season based on their records (103-59 vs. 100-62) and run differentials (+214 vs. +201), and they certainly played like the better team in the NLCS. The better team doesn't always win a postseason series. In the NLCS though, the better team has played like the better team, period.
2. Shohei Ohtani
MLB's brightest star was greatly dimmed ... even with Game 4 homer
The biggest star on baseball's most star-laden team was not himself the last two months of the season. Shohei Ohtani played through knee and biceps injuries and had been so unproductive than Roberts said there would at least be a "conversation" about sitting Ohtani in Game 3. That didn't come to pass, and hey, Ohtani went 1 for 2 with a walk and a hit-by-pitch in Game 3, and hit a home run in Game 4. The homer put the Dodgers up 4-0 on Thursday. The Dodgers didn't score again. The bottom line is Ohtani was a non-factor until it was too late. It's hard to win when your best player is this diminished.
Whenever a team loses in the postseason, the best player gets a disproportionate amount of the blame, and that applies to Ohtani this series. He's clearly not healthy, , and he's had multiple chances in the first three games to swing things in his team's favor, but couldn't do it. When the best player underperforms, he wears most of the blame. It has been the way of the world since the dawn of team sports.
3. Freddie Freeman
Normally clutch, Freeman has been the worst player in the series
Freddie Freeman, not Ohtani, was the worst player in the NLCS by both win probability added and championship probability added. He went 1 for 14 in the series and the one hit came in the first inning of Game 1. Freeman went 0 for 13 after his first NLCS at-bat and that 0 for 13 includes:
- Striking out after Mookie Betts worked a leadoff walk in the third inning of Game 1.
- Grounding into an inning-ending double play in the fifth inning of Game 1.
- Popping up to second on the first pitch to lead off the eighth inning of Game 1.
- Flying out with runners on first and second and no outs in the third inning of Game 2.
- Flying out with runners on first and second and one out in the third inning of Game 3.
- Grounding out with a runner on first and two outs in the fifth inning of Game 3.
That's an awful lot of empty at-bats in clutch situations for one of the best clutch hitters of this generation. Freeman had as many double plays as total bases (one each) in the NLCS, and his only RBI came on a sacrifice fly. You won't beat a team as good as the Brewers with sac flies. You need bigger swings from your best players and Freeman didn't provide them.
4. The supporting cast
Only two Dodgers hitters had consistently strong at-bats in the NLCS
Max Muncy went 2 for 12 with six strikeouts in the NLCS. Teoscar Hernández went 3 for 14. Andy Pages went 3 for 12. Tommy Edman went 1 for 7. Will Smith went 2 for 15 in the NLCS. Postseason legend Enrique Hernández went 0 for 8 with a ghasty strikeout in Game 3. The Dodgers had runners at second and third with one out in sixth, and Hernández took two pitches in the zone for strikes, then flailed at slider out of the zone. It was maybe the single worst at-bat of this NLCS.
Freeman was terrible, Ohtani was terrible, and the thing that has so often set the Dodgers apart these last few years -- an elite supporting cast -- was terrible as well. Edman, Muncy, Smith, and the Hernándezes are a combined 11 for 58 (.189) in the four games. Betts (3 for 15 with three walks) and Kyle Tucker (4 for 12 with three walks) were the only Dodgers hitters who escaped scrutiny. They were their most productive hitters and consistently had strong at-bats. Everyone else? 😴😴😴
5. Dave Roberts
Roberts did not push the right buttons
The manager can not swing the bat or throw the ball for his players, but he can put his team in the best position to succeed, and Roberts did not do that in the NLCS. Game 3, especially, was a managerial mess. Roberts burned the precocious Josue De Paula in the sixth inning when he sent him up to pinch-hit for Miguel Rojas with runners on second and third and one out, then immediately pinch-hit Enrique Hernández for De Paula when the Brewers brought in a lefty reliever.
De Paula is a rookie, I get that, but he has a track record of hitting lefties well in the minors. More accurately, he has a strong track record of making contact against lefties, which is what the Dodgers needed in that spot. A ball in play to get a run home. Instead, Roberts defaulted to the veteran Hernández, who struck out feebly. For all his career postseason success, Hernández went 1 for 14 this postseason, and a .190/.235/.317 hitter in his last 19 postseason games. Roberts never adjusted his priors.
The NLCS was a flashback to pre-2024 Roberts, when he too often showed too much faith in his veterans and had an unfortunate knack for sticking with starters too long. In 2024 and 2025, it all worked out, and Roberts looked like a genius. Those same mistakes, the ones he got away with the last two years, reared their ugly heads. The NLCS sweep is on the players, first and foremost. Roberts didn't play his cards well either. He's made things worse.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers face an offseason reckoning after stunning NLCS sweep
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: The home run shredded the October sky like a bolt of lightning. Shohei Ohtani turned toward the Dodgers’ bench. He threw his bat. He screamed. He punched the air. He screamed some more. With one furious swing, Ohtani unleashed months of pent-up frustration. His streak of 115 plate appearances without a home run was over. But this wasn’t a series-altering three-run home run. This was a last stand. The four-run lead the Dodgers built up in that stadium-rocking second inning didn’t endure. The Milw
item.content:encoded:
The home run shredded the October sky like a bolt of lightning.
Shohei Ohtani turned toward the Dodgers’ bench.
He threw his bat. He screamed. He punched the air. He screamed some more.
With one furious swing, Ohtani unleashed months of pent-up frustration.
His streak of 115 plate appearances without a home run was over.
But this wasn’t a series-altering three-run home run.
This was a last stand.
The four-run lead the Dodgers built up in that stadium-rocking second inning didn’t endure. The Milwaukee Brewers saw that it wouldn’t.
As they did throughout this National League Championship Series, the Brewers pressed and pressed and pressed. Little by little, the Dodgers gave in.
By the sixth inning, the Dodgers were behind. Three innings later, they were officially eliminated from the playoffs when Kiké Hernández flied out to left field against Aaron Ashby for the final out of a 6-4 defeat at Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers didn’t just lose.
They were swept in four games by the same team they swept at this stage of the postseason last year.
Now, comes the hard part.
The Dodgers might be the second-best team in baseball behind the Brewers, but they can’t return with a similar roster next season and expect the results to be any different.
Farewells are in order.
Farewell to long-time Dodgers who will forever be known in these parts as World Series heroes.
Farewell to Ohtani hitting and pitching full-time.
With how the Dodgers were thumped by the Brewers, president of baseball operation Andrew Friedman has a clear directive.
Adjust – or else.
The Dodgers have the oldest team in the major leagues. First baseman Freddie Freeman and infielder Miguel Rojas are 37. Third baseman Max Muncy is 36 and utilityman Kiké Hernández is 35. Shortstop Mookie Betts and outfielder Teoscar Hernández are 34.
The problem is magnified by their prime-aged players, who are breaking down as if they are senior citizens.
Ohtani, 32, was obviously debilitated in the postseason, which explains why a former 50-homer player wasn’t a power threat for the majority of these playoffs.
Catcher Will Smith, 31, was sidelined for three months with a disc problem, which contributed to him being out of sorts in the batter’s box.
Utilityman Tommy Edman, also 31, is an All-Star-caliber player when healthy – but he often isn’t.
Kyle Tucker, 29, flat-out stunk for the majority of the first season of his four-year, $240-million contract.
What Friedman and others in the front office will have to decide in the coming weeks and months is how quickly and drastically they will turn over the roster.
The Dodgers shopped Teoscar Hernández last offseason, and they figure to do so again this offseason, as they already have a promising in-house replacement for him in left field in 21-year-old rookie Josue De Paula. Hernández has only one more guaranteed year remaining on his contract.
But what do the Dodgers do beyond that?
Do they attempt to move some of their other veterans? Or do they field more or less the same team next season, accept the limitations of their roster, and wait for some of their contracts to expire in another year?
Freeman will be an unrestricted free agent after the 2027 season. Muncy could also depart that winter, as his option for the 2028 season is a team option.
There are no simple answers.
Muncy’s option for 2028 is a relative bargain at $10 million, for example. The Dodgers might not be able to find a better third baseman at that price point.
Or, in the case of Freeman, how can they not re-sign a player as beloved as he is?
One factor that could influence the Dodgers’ team-building approach: Baseball’s next collective-bargaining agreement.
More restrictive spending limits of some kind figure to be on their way, as franchise owners are pushing for a salary cap. The Dodgers could be forced to dump salaries whether they want to or not.
Whatever happens on that front, the Dodgers will have to address Ohtani’s situation.
Ohtani broke into Japan’s top league as an 18 year old. He was a two-way player in the five seasons he played for the Nippon-Ham Fighters, and his body has plenty of mileage on it.
This season was particularly demanding.
Last year, resumed pitching in the middle of the season after recovering from his second major elbow operation. This year, he attempted to be a full-time hitter and pitcher for the entire season.
Ohtani broke down. He abandoned pitching in the middle of the season. The resulting injuries diminished him as a hitter.
Knowing Ohtani will insist on remaining a two-way player, what do the Dodgers do?
Do they spread out his starts to extend the periods between his starts? Or do they try to sell him on the idea that by not pitching in the early parts of the season, he could be a two-way player in October?
The results have spoken.
Changes will have to be made.

item.title: [Sportsnet.ca] Brewers sweep Dodgers in NLCS to book ticket to World Series
item.dc:creator: Ben Nicholson-Smith
item.description: LOS ANGELES — With the score tied at four in the top of the sixth inning, Tanner Scott threw a fastball down the middle and Garrett Mitchell crushed it. As the ball soared over the centre field wall at Dodger Stadium, reality set in for the two-time defending champions and their fans: their reign atop MLB might be ending. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — With the score tied at four in the top of the sixth inning, Tanner Scott threw a fastball down the middle and Garrett Mitchell crushed it.
As the ball soared over the centre field wall at Dodger Stadium, reality set in for the two-time defending champions and their fans: their reign atop MLB might be ending. And a few innings later, when Aaron Ashby retired Kiké Hernandez for the final out of a 6-4 win in Game 4 of the NLCS, it was all over.
There were late chances to score Kyle Tucker from second and Will Smith from third, but in the end the Dodgers failed.
They’re a great team, but not the best team in baseball anymore, or even the best team in the National League. That honour goes to the Milwaukee Brewers, who secured the pennant with a sweep of the Dodgers thanks to Mitchell’s big swing, some tenacious rallies in the middle innings and impressive relief pitching.
The win overshadowed a dramatic home run from Shohei Ohtani and disappointed 49,104 fans still hoping for a third straight championship. Instead, it’s Milwaukee who will represent the National League in the World Series in a battle of small markets against either Cleveland or Tampa Bay.
All series, the Brewers outplayed the Dodgers. They hit more home runs, they played better defence and they pitched better. And really, that should come as no surprise. This team has reached the post-season eight of the last nine seasons, including each of the last four NL Central titles.
But still, the Dodgers are baseball’s preeminent team, so when Shohei Ohtani demolished a Dustin May cutter to give the Dodgers an early 4-0 lead, their path to victory seemed to open up again. As the ball soared into the right-field bleachers, Ohtani bounced backwards towards first base and yelled at his teammates in the third-base dugout. It may be the most emotion he’s ever shown on a big-league field.
Considering the context, Ohtani’s home run was all the more significant. Just two days ago, there was talk of benching him given his middling performance and knee and biceps injuries. Then came a stellar performance in Game 3 and his Game 4 home run, the first one he’s hit since August 18.
But aside from Ohtani’s big swing, the Dodgers simply didn’t have answers offensively. No one else homered in the NLCS. In fact, they had just five other extra-base hits this series — all doubles. A team known for its high-powered offence had produced backup-catcher type numbers when it counted most.
They needed to hit or see their season end, no in-between. And they didn’t hit, so their season ended.
The Brewers, on the other hand, managed just enough offence. David Hamilton added a late home run and breakout star Jake Bauers drove in three, including two with a pivotal double in the fourth inning. All series, they found answers against the Dodgers team that allowed the fewest runs in MLB this regular season.
Oddly enough, this will be the first time the Brewers represent the National League in the World Series. When they made it in 1982, they were still an American League team and lost to the Cardinals in seven games.
The Dodgers were seeking the first MLB three-peat since the 1998-2000 Yankees and only the fifth in MLB history (Athletics 1972-74; Yankees 1949-53; Yankees 1936-39). Instead, they’ll turn their attention to the off-season, with Hernandez, Miguel Rojas, Alex Vesia and, most notably, Tarik Skubal all headed for free agency.
Before then, the Brewers will participate in a World Series featuring two of MLB’s lowest payrolls, undermining the narrative that MLB needs a salary cap for small-market teams to compete. The Brewers didn’t just beat the Dodgers, they dominated them thanks to elite player acquisition, strong player development and a strong team culture.
Soon enough, more tests await the Brewers. First, though, it’s time for a well deserved celebration.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Dodgers Gamble On Ex-Tigers Pitcher Tarik Skubal Backfires

item.content:encoded:
Earlier this season, the Detroit Tigers made the difficult decision to part ways with ace pitcher Tarik Skubal, sending him to the defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers in return for a package that included a trio of prospects.
While the Tigers missed the playoffs, the Dodgers once again advanced to the National League Championship Series, but their dreams of a three-peat were broken by the upstart Milwaukee Brewers.
In a stunning result, the Brewers swept Tarik Skubal and the Dodgers in four games, advancing to the World Series for the first time since 1982.
Former Detroit Tigers Ace Tarik Skubal And The Los Angeles Dodgers Were Swept In The NLCS
The run for Skubal and the Dodgers this season ended in extreme disappointment, as the New York Yankees remain the most recent club to capture three straight World Series wins.
It was Skubal who started the first game of the NLCS against the Brewers; while he delivered an acceptable performance, he didn’t get much run support. He allowed just two earned runs on five hits and two walks with seven strikeouts over 5.0 innings of work in what was a 2-1 loss.
Now, the Dodgers are faced with an uncertain future with regard to Skubal, who can become an unrestricted free agent and is expected to command a historic contract negotiated by power agent Scott Boras potentially worth upward of $400 million.
Whether or not the Dodgers are able to keep Skubal remains to be seen.
The Tigers Traded Tarik Skubal To The Dodgers
In return for Skubal, the Tigers received outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith.
“We came into this with a firm idea of the type of deal that we wanted to ultimately land,” said Tigers executive Scott Harris after the trade. “And we had a deep understanding of what every organization had to offer.
“I think there is a unique dynamic with a player like Tarik Skubal. Markets at the deadline for the top players are just different than the rest of the market. So, I understand the intuition that, ‘Hey, you’re supposed to wait until the very last second on a deal and then pull a trigger at the very last second to maximize a return.’ That’s not how markets for the top players work.”

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers’ manager Dave Roberts told reporters on Thursday that he’s very unlikely to use Tarik Skubal or Yoshinobu Yamamoto out of the bullpen in Game 4 of the NLCS against the Brewers.

Even with their backs against the wall, Roberts maintained confidence when asked if his star hurlers would be available out of the bullpen on Thursday, saying, “No. ... Our bullpen is rested, very, very capable. You’ve still got to win four, but obviously you’ve got to win one first, and I completely understand that. But the short answer, no.” It’s possible that the calculus could change if the Dodgers get down early in Game 4, but for now he appears to have full faith in Tyler Glasnow and his rested bullpen.

item.title: [FOX Sports] Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4
item.description: Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4 One loss from elimination, the Los Angeles Dodgers restored Shohei Ohtani to the top of the batting order for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night. item.content:encoded:
Dodgers Move Shohei Ohtani Back To Leadoff With Season On Line In NLCS Game 4
One loss from elimination, the Los Angeles Dodgers restored Shohei Ohtani to the top of the batting order for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night.
The Dodgers trailed the Milwaukee Brewers 3-0 in the best-of-seven series, and needed to four straight wins to reach the World Series and keep alive their bid for a third consecutive championship.
Ohtani batted sixth in a 6-2 loss on Wednesday night, the lowest he's hit since joining the Dodgers ahead of the 2024 season. He was 1 for 2 with a walk to raise his batting average to .182.
"Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at," manager Dave Roberts said before the game. "I liked the at-bats yesterday. Obviously we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to."
(Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images)
Ohtani typically leads off the order but has been dropped lower while struggling with injuries to his left knee and right biceps for the last few months. Roberts didn't tell Ohtani about the change before posting the lineup.
Roberts said Ohtani has given him reasons to believe in the four-time MVP, citing Ohtani staying until 9 p.m. on Tuesday to work on his swing and his improved at-bat quality.
"Baking all that in, I felt absolutely, put him at the top," he said. "I feel good about him taking five at-bats and giving us our best chance to win and produce runs."
Roberts tweaked the entire lineup after Wednesday's loss put the Dodgers on the brink of elimination. Mookie Betts, who led off in Game 3, was bumped to No. 2, while Freddie Freeman moved to No. 3.
Will Smith, whose offensive struggles mirrored Ohtani's, moved up to fourth from seventh. Smith doubled in the sixth inning, when the Dodgers briefly took a 2-1 lead.
"I thought Will took very good at-bats, big hit yesterday," Roberts said. "He’s been in big spots."
Kyle Tucker hit fifth, while Teoscar Hernandez went from third to sixth. Miguel Rojas hit seventh and Andy Pages dropped to eighth from fifth.
Kiké Hernández, who came off the bench in Game 3, hit ninth, with regular third baseman Max Muncy available to come off the bench for Rojas or Kiké Hernández.
Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Struggling Shohei Ohtani back in leadoff spot as Dodgers face elimination
item.description: One day after being dropped to sixth in the batting order, Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani is back in the leadoff spot for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night. The Milwaukee Brewers won the first three games of the series and can clinch a World Series berth on Thursday night in Los Angeles. With elimination facing the Dodgers, manager Dave Roberts put Ohtani back atop the order for the first time since the final game of the regular season on Sept. 27. In We
item.content:encoded:
One day after being dropped to sixth in the batting order, Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani is back in the leadoff spot for Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night.
The Milwaukee Brewers won the first three games of the series and can clinch a World Series berth on Thursday night in Los Angeles.
With elimination facing the Dodgers, manager Dave Roberts put Ohtani back atop the order for the first time since the final game of the regular season on Sept. 27. In Wednesday’s 6-2 loss, Ohtani went 1-for-2 with a walk and a hit by pitch.
“Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at,” Roberts said prior to Game 4. “I just really — I liked the at-bats yesterday, and I felt that trying to shake it up a little bit. Obviously, we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit, but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to.”
Ohtani, 32, has been bothered by right biceps and left knee injuries for multiple months and his productivity has slipped.
He has batted just .182 (4-for-22) with no homers and no RBIs in seven postseason games. Ohtani hasn’t homered since Aug. 18 against the Colorado Rockies and owns just one RBI since that homer.
When he batted sixth against the Brewers on Wednesday, it marked the first time he had batted so low in a starting lineup since Sept. 19, 2020 – when the Los Angeles Angels slotted him sixth as the designated hitter against the Texas Rangers.
Roberts said he didn’t tell Ohtani in advance about his return to the leadoff spot. He likes the idea of it possibly jump-starting Ohtani and his struggling troops.
“I feel good about him taking five at-bats and giving us our best chance to win and produce runs today,” Roberts said of Ohtani.
Ohtani is a four-time MVP — twice with the Angels and twice with the Dodgers — during nine big league campaigns. He hit 11 postseason homers, including eight last year, as the Dodgers won back-to-back titles.
–Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
En las Grandes Ligas de Béisbol (MLB), pocas historias representan mejor la capacidad de resistir bajo presión que la protagonizada por los Red Sox de Boston en 2004. Hace exactamente 22 años, todo parecía perdido frente a los Yankees de Nueva York —su máximo rival—, pero los de Boston encontraron la manera de transformar una eliminación prácticamente anunciada en una de las hazañas más recordadas de la historia del béisbol.
Más de dos décadas después, aquella remontada vuelve a cobrar relevancia, siendo referencia para unos Dodgers de Los Ángeles que también se encuentran al borde del abismo en su camino al tricampeonato consecutivo.
Una remontada para la historia
La Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana de 2004 comenzó con un dominio contundente de los Yankees. Nueva York ganó los primeros tres encuentros y dejó a Boston contra las cuerdas, a una sola derrota de despedirse de la postemporada. El panorama parecía todavía más oscuro después del tercer partido, cuando los neoyorquinos se impusieron por un escandaloso 19-8.
Sin embargo, los Red Sox se negaron a aceptar su destino. Boston ganó el cuarto encuentro por 6-4 en entradas extras —lo que le añadió todavía más drama a la casi eliminación— y volvió a imponerse en el quinto, también en episodios adicionales, por 5-4. Con la confianza recuperada, llegó otro 4-2 a los Yankees en el sexto juego, para luego sellar la remontada con una contundente victoria de 10-3 en el séptimo, disputado incluso fuera de casa, en el Yankee Stadium.
Aquella reacción tuvo varios protagonistas inolvidables. David Ortiz apareció en los momentos decisivos y fue nombrado “Jugador Más Valioso” (MVP) de la serie. Johnny Damon también dejó su huella en el partido definitivo, con dos cuadrangulares y seis carreras impulsadas. Pero hubo otro nombre que quedó ligado para siempre al inicio de aquella transformación: nada más y nada menos que Dave Roberts.
El actual mánager de los Dodgers era entonces corredor emergente de Boston. En el noveno episodio del cuarto juego, con su equipo al borde de la eliminación, se robó la segunda base ante Mariano Rivera. Minutos después anotó la carrera del empate, en lo que fue una jugada que cambió el rumbo de la serie y le abrió la puerta a una remontada sin precedentes.
El significado de aquella reacción fue mucho más allá de una serie de playoffs. Boston terminó conquistando la Serie Mundial de 2004 barriendo a los St. Louis Cardinals, y poniendo fin a una espera de 86 años sin levantar el trofeo más importante. La llamada “Maldición del Bambino” quedó atrás y los Red Sox cambiaron para siempre la historia de su franquicia.
Veintidós años después, Roberts vuelve a encontrarse frente a un 0-3, aunque esta vez desde el banquillo. Sus Dodgers perdieron los primeros tres partidos de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional ante los Brewers.
El golpe más reciente llegó con el triunfo de los de Milwaukee por 6-2 en el tercer encuentro, después de que Jake Bauers y Garrett Mitchell conectaran cuadrangulares consecutivos en la séptima entrada, silenciando un Dodger Stadium que segundos antes había celebrado con locura un inning de dos carreras para ponerse 2-1 al frente.
La derrota dejó a Los Ángeles sin margen de error. Pese a contar con figuras como Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts y Freddie Freeman, los Dodgers necesitan recuperar la producción ofensiva y encontrar respuestas ante un rival que ha sabido aprovechar sus oportunidades.
Los Brewers, por su parte, están a una victoria de regresar a la Serie Mundial por primera vez desde 1982. Milwaukee tiene la ventaja, el impulso y la oportunidad de cerrar la serie.
Los Ángeles, en cambio, ya no puede mirar más allá del siguiente partido. Necesita ganar cuatro encuentros consecutivos para sobrevivir y avanzar a la Serie Mundial, y la experiencia de Roberts convierte la comparación con 2004 en algo inevitable. Él sabe de primera mano que ir en contra 0-3 no significa una eliminación matemática, pero también conoce el tamaño del reto. Aquellos Red Sox demostraron cómo una sola victoria puede cambiar la presión de lado y transformar por completo una serie.
La comparación, sin embargo, tiene límites. Los Red Sox de 2004 ya escribieron su nombre en los libros de récords al convertirse en el único equipo que ha remontado un marcador así en una serie de postemporada al mejor de siete juegos. Los Dodgers todavía deben demostrar que pueden acompañarlos en la historia.
La pregunta ahora es si Roberts podrá convertir sus recuerdos de 2004 en una fuente de inspiración para su equipo. Hace 22 años, Dave Roberts ayudó a encender una remontada que parecía imposible. Hoy, su misión es intentar que aquella historia no sea solamente un recuerdo glorioso, sino el ejemplo de que todavía queda una última oportunidad para cambiar el destino.

item.title: [MLB.com] Back to basics: Ohtani returns to leadoff spot for NLCS Game 4
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- With their season on the line, the Dodgers are going back to their roots. Shohei Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for the first time this postseason as the Dodgers shook up their lineup ahead of Game 4 of the NL Championship Series against the Brewers on Thursday night at Dodger Stadium, a game they must win to keep their season -- and their three-peat bid -- alive. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- With their season on the line, the Dodgers are going back to their roots.
Shohei Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for the first time this postseason as the Dodgers shook up their lineup ahead of Game 4 of the NL Championship Series against the Brewers on Thursday night at Dodger Stadium, a game they must win to keep their season -- and their three-peat bid -- alive.
Ohtani dropped as low as sixth in the order in NLCS Game 3, when a scuffling Will Smith also dropped to seventh. Both contributed to the Dodgers' lone run-scoring rally in the sixth inning, with Ohtani drawing a walk to load the bases before Smith cashed in with a two-run double. Two innings later, Ohtani smoked a 113.5 mph single, his hardest-hit batted ball since June 20.
The big plate appearances from Ohtani and Smith, as well as the work they have put in behind the scenes, were enough to convince manager Dave Roberts to elevate both of them back up the order.
"I think getting back to what we've done all year and how it's been going recently as far as on the offense," Roberts said, "I think it warranted just a little bit of a shakeup."
Here's the full lineup:
1. Shohei Ohtani, DH
2. Mookie Betts, SS
3. Freddie Freeman, 1B
4. Will Smith, C
5. Kyle Tucker, RF
6. Teoscar Hernández, LF
7. Miguel Rojas, 2B
8. Andy Pages, CF
9. Kiké Hernández, 3B
The Dodgers are trying to do what just one other team has done before: Come back from being down 0-3 in a best-of-seven postseason series. Of the 42 teams that have been in that position, only Roberts' 2004 Red Sox have successfully come back to win the series. Thirty-two of those series ended in sweeps.
Roberts' advice to his team is to focus solely on winning Game 4. They can't look at the big picture of needing four wins in as many games. They need to win each pitch, each inning and each day for as long as their season is alive.
Having Ohtani back atop the order, Roberts hopes, will put the Dodgers in the best position to do that. Ohtani is hitting 4-for-22 (.182) with no extra-base hits, seven strikeouts and four walks in seven games this postseason. There was a discussion about sitting him for Game 3 amid his lingering right biceps and left knee injuries, but Ohtani was adamant that he felt good enough to play and was close to figuring something out with his swing.
The reasoning for Ohtani's return to the leadoff spot a game later is twofold: He showed Roberts enough through his work and in Game 3. And if this is it for the Dodgers' postseason run, Roberts wants to go down trusting his generational talent to set the tone.
"There is something to that, absolutely," Roberts said. "But also I think the player still has to give you hope to believe in, to bet on -- where I think that the work, being here till 9 p.m. two nights ago working, the at-bats yesterday. For me baking all that in, I felt absolutely, put him at the top."

item.title: [Reviewing the Brew] Everything Brewers fans need to know about Dodgers’ Game 4 starter Tyler Glasnow

Alas, the Crew will have to get through Tyler Glasnow if they want to complete their revenge arc and sweep the two-time reigning champs in the NLCS. item.content:encoded:
It's sort of a sick joke that, even down 3-0 and having used up their trio of all-universe aces, the Los Angeles Dodgers can trot another frontline starter out to the mound to try and stave off elimination against the Milwaukee Brewers. Alas, the Crew will have to get through Tyler Glasnow if they want to complete their revenge arc and sweep the two-time reigning champs in the NLCS.
Of course, after seeing Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and Blake Snell -- who have four Cy Youngs and a World Series MVP between them -- there's not much that should faze the Brewers. Glasnow is a very good pitcher, but he's the closest thing to a weak link in the Dodgers' super-rotation.
Still, he's an intimidating presence on the bump and has had tons of success against most of Pat Murphy's lineup to boot. Milwaukee will counter with rookie southpaw Shane Drohan, though this will be an all-hands-on-deck effort as the Brewers try to get to where they haven't been since 1982.
To sweep Dodgers, Brewers will need to overcome intimidating history against Tyler Glasnow
Let's start with the optimistic view. Glasnow remains a perpetually injury-prone pitcher, making just 13 starts this year while dealing with back spasms and various setbacks. Though that means his arm should be fresh, he also likely isn't operating at 100%; his last start (against the Braves in the NLDS) saw him yield only one hit across 4⅔ innings, but he also walked five batters as part of a laborious outing.
That's an exploitable weakness the Crew need to take advantage of, since Glasnow has walked multiple batters in each of his past five starts. Running up his pitch count early will force Dave Roberts to dig into his stash of relievers, many of whom seemingly don't have his trust right now.
The major concern for the Brewers lies in the past, since Glasnow has had their number historically. Christian Yelich (one hit, seven strikeouts in 14 plate appearances), William Contreras (zero hits in 10 PAs), and Jackson Chourio (.286 OPS in seven PAs) have all struggled mightily in their head-to-head matchups with the right-hander.
Those numbers also don't include his dominant performance in Game 3 of last year's NLCS, when he struck out eight and held the Brewers to one run on three hits over 5⅔ innings. As such, the work of Game 3 hero Jake Bauers (.952 OPS in seven PAs) and Brice Turang (.375 OBP in eight PAs) will be key to getting the Crew ahead tonight.
Having already taken down all of the Dodgers' best arms, the Brewers should enter this one with immense confidence. With a trip to the World Series on the line, all they need to do is crush their Tyler Glasnow demons.

item.title: [Motor City Bengals] Checking in on the Tigers' Tarik Skubal return as the Dodgers stare down elimination
item.dc:creator: Anthony Ranaudo
item.description: It's bittersweet to watch someone you loved for so long pitch in October for another team, especially one that could win a championship. Tarik Skubal won two Cy Youngs in a Tigers uniform, and now he's chasing a ring with the Dodgers, who trail the Brewers 3-0 in the NLCS. LA needs three wins in a row just to get to a Game 7, and a fourth just to get to the World Series. It's a steep climb, and if it ends this week, the conversation in Detroit shifts quickly from what was lost to what was gained
item.content:encoded:
It's bittersweet to watch someone you loved for so long pitch in October for another team, especially one that could win a championship. Tarik Skubal won two Cy Youngs in a Tigers uniform, and now he's chasing a ring with the Dodgers, who trail the Brewers 3-0 in the NLCS.
LA needs three wins in a row just to get to a Game 7, and a fourth just to get to the World Series. It's a steep climb, and if it ends this week, the conversation in Detroit shifts quickly from what was lost to what was gained.
How the Tigers' Skubal trade return looks heading into 2027
The package was Zyhir Hope, River Ryan and Brady Smith, and each one is in a different place right now, starting with the centerpiece. Hope recently kicked off his stint in the highly-touted Arizona Fall League, and is off to a nice start. Through six games with Scottsdale he's hitting .286 with an .873 OPS, five walks, eight strikeouts and five RBI. He hit his first homer on Monday, a two-run shot at 101 MPH.
However, it wasn't all smooth at the outset for Hope when he was traded over. MLB.com noted he had "plenty of adjusting to do" with a new organization and lineup, and after a very slow start, his Double-A line with Erie (.269/.360/.462) wound up being not as pretty as what he'd done at Tulsa (.293/.369/.530). He crushed the ball in September and still wrapped up the 2026 season with 29 homers, 26 steals and 111 RBI, and went deep in the Eastern League finals.
This AFL start is a small sample (and will be, no matter how good or bad it goes), especially after a career-high 564 plate appearances, but it's an encouraging sign. As for 2027, there's a lot of excitement around the organization about how he can contribute, and when he will arrive in Detroit. Still, it's worth not piling expectations on a young player. Time will tell, and the Tigers will give him plenty of opportunity.
The most immediate return is River Ryan, who has already pitched for the big-league club. He debuted on September 21 with three scoreless innings against the Nationals, and closed the year with a 4.15 ERA and six strikeouts over 4⅓ innings in two starts. That's a tiny sample, so the numbers behind it are worth a look. He throws six pitches, and all of them are average or above average according to Stuff+. And he commands them: in Triple-A this year he struck out 10.3 per nine while walking just 2.0.
There may be some injury concern as he's coming back from Tommy John surgery and a hamstring injury this past year, and really since 2024. And although it was that small sample size, his two MLB starts included 6.2 walks per nine, which is a bit alarming. But his lengthy Triple-A numbers make me feel better. No matter what, the stuff and the strike-throwing are why people are excited, and if he stays healthy he should be penciled into the 2027 rotation.
Health is also the story with Smith. He made two starts for High-A West Michigan before leaving his second in the second inning after five batters and a visit from a trainer, and he went on the injured list August 20. With Tommy John surgery in his past, I'd bet they shut him down as a precaution and are aiming for a healthy 2027. If he is, I'd expect him to move up to Double-A at some point, and since he came over in the Skubal trade, the organization should give him plenty of runway to get to the big leagues.
That's the thing about this trade. It's fun to watch Skubal even when it hurts to see him in another uniform, but between Hope's bat, Ryan's arm and Smith's upside, the 2027-and-beyond picture is exciting too. And if the Dodgers can't manage a comeback, it's even sweeter.

item.title: [reviewingthebrew.com] Brewers' best (and only) chance for historic playoff redemption in NLCS is in Shane Drohan's hands
item.dc:creator: Owen Jonas
item.description: Much of the media's attention heading into this year's NLCS rematch between the Milwaukee Brewers and Los Angeles Dodgers was on the strength of the defending World Series Champions' starting pitching group. With a pair of Cy Young-winning left-handers in Tarik Skubal, whom the Dodgers acquired at the midseason trade deadline, and Blake Snell, as well as 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto and All-Star right-hander Tyler Glasnow in their rotation, that attention was well-deserved. However,
item.content:encoded:
Much of the media's attention heading into this year's NLCS rematch between the Milwaukee Brewers and Los Angeles Dodgers was on the strength of the defending World Series Champions' starting pitching group. With a pair of Cy Young-winning left-handers in Tarik Skubal, whom the Dodgers acquired at the midseason trade deadline, and Blake Snell, as well as 2025 World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto and All-Star right-hander Tyler Glasnow in their rotation, that attention was well-deserved.
However, through the first three games of the NLCS, the Brewers have bested Los Angeles' top three starters and built a commanding 3-0 series lead. Skubal and Snell took the loss in Games 1 and 3, respectively, and sandwiched in between was a 2.2-inning, 75-pitch start from Yamamoto that forced Dave Roberts to use seven relief pitchers in Game 2. On the other side, Milwaukee's starting group hasn't necessarily been the strength of their pitching staff during the postseason -- that would be their bullpen -- but the trio of Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson, and Robert Gasser combined for 13.1 innings and allowed just two earned runs through the first three NLCS games.
Game 4 is where things get interesting. While the Brewers' decision to start Miz, Henderson, and Gasser in the first three games of the NLCS felt like an obvious one, especially after Gasser's strong showing in the NLDS, who would get the ball to start Game 4 remained an unanswered question through this morning.
However, just moments ago, the Brewers officially revealed that rookie southpaw Shane Drohan will start Game 4 of the NLCS tonight. Drohan, who will be making his postseason debut, will be the first out-getter of Milwaukee's quest for never-before-seen level of redemption in a playoff series.
Brewers trying to become first team in MLB history to sweep a team in the playoffs who swept them in the previous postseason
The Brewers just have to win one of their next four games to return to the World Series for the first time since 1982. That much is true. That said, closing out the Dodgers tonight and completing one of the most impressive sweeps in postseason history would be a redemption performance never before seen in MLB history. According to MLB.com's statistician Sarah Langs, no team in the history of MLB has swept a team in a postseason series after being swept by that same team in the previous playoffs.
After the demoralizing loss that the Brewers suffered in last year's NLCS, defeating the Dodgers in four games this year would easily be one of the most satisfying postseason series sweeps in MLB history. Pair that with the payroll disparity that exists between the two clubs, the fact that Los Angeles is pursuing a three-peat, and the Dodgers' victory in the Tarik Skubal trade deadline sweepstakes, and the Brewers sweeping MLB's Evil Empire would be especially gratifying.
Completing that sweep in Game 4 tonight starts with a strong showing from Drohan, who hasn't pitched in any of the Brewers' first seven postseason games this year. Drohan impressed during the regular season, with a 4.19 ERA in 124.2 innings to prove it. His low arm-slot from the left side matches up well with Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman, and his six-pitch mix should keep the struggling Dodgers' offense off-balance.
It likely won't be a long start for Drohan, especially given the arms available in Pat Murphy's 'pen. In theory, only DL Hall is unavailable for tonight's game, but the Brewers may elect to avoid using Abner Uribe for an eighth consecutive game as well. However, that leaves Kyle Harrison, Dustin May, Chad Patrick, Aaron Ashby, Antonio Senzatela, JoJo Romero, and Trevor Megill available for Murphy to turn to after Drohan.
Any type of victory over the Dodgers in this year's NLCS would represent redemption for the Brewers after being swept by Los Angeles a season ago. However, Milwaukee's only shot at historic redemption that has never occurred in the history of MLB is tonight, during which rookie southpaw Shane Drohan will kick off their sweep attempt.

item.title: [si.com] Brewers Are Using Postseason Stage to Showcase MLB’s New Era
item.dc:creator: Tom Verducci
item.description: Los Angeles — When dynasties fall, it is not insurrection, nor jealousy, nor sloth that bring them down. It is the undefeated champion of the world, Father Time. We are watching the Los Angeles Dodgers age out. The Milwaukee Brewers proved for a third time in the National League Championship Series they are the better (and younger) team, completing a beautiful triptych of comebacks with a 6-2 win in Game 3 on Wednesday. In three successive games, the Dodgers had Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles — When dynasties fall, it is not insurrection, nor jealousy, nor sloth that bring them down. It is the undefeated champion of the world, Father Time. We are watching the Los Angeles Dodgers age out.
The Milwaukee Brewers proved for a third time in the National League Championship Series they are the better (and younger) team, completing a beautiful triptych of comebacks with a 6-2 win in Game 3 on Wednesday. In three successive games, the Dodgers had Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Blake Snell on the mound with a lead and lost all three. Ninety-five million dollars, four Cy Young awards and a World Series MVP worth of pitching and they could not hold back Milwaukee any more than you can hold back water with your hands.
But the most obvious reason why the Brewers have put the Dodger dynasty on the brink of extinction is this: the youngest pitching staff in baseball—and the hardest throwing staff in postseason history—has smothered the oldest team in baseball. Milwaukee is pushing around the aging Dodgers lineup with a barrage of fastballs in three versions, especially power sinkers. They are shoving 66.8% fastballs at the Dodgers at an average velocity of 97.9 mph. The Dodgers’ only path to victory is to slug and the Brewers simply won’t allow it.
“I just think they’re really good pitchers,” Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas said. “A lot of their pitchers throw three different fastballs. They throw hard, and they’ve been locating the ball really well. They haven’t really given us too much of an opportunity to kind of build momentum.
“They’ve been attacking the zone. They throw their stuff in the zone—and with all three fastballs. A lot of guys have a cutter, a sinker and a four-seam fastball. It’s really hard to put barrels on the ball.
“At the end of the day, it’s just the velocity of their stuff. They throw the ball really hard. And we all know when you throw that hard, it’s really hard.”
The Brewers knew coming into the series that in today’s game older players don’t hit elite fastballs as well as younger players, and so the matchup was to their liking. But this? Who could have seen this in the NLCS? The Dodgers:
- Have two extra-base hits in 105 plate appearances
- Have been outhomered, 5-0
- Are the first team in franchise history to lose three straight games in one postseason with no home runs and no attempted stolen bases
- Are hitting .228 against fastballs
- Are 2-for-16 with runners in scoring position, part of a 3-for-32 postseason disaster in those spots
This has been the year in which baseball made a sharp turn when it comes to the speed of the game. Younger players thrive. Velocity, and the widespread adoption of the family of three fastballs, changed everything. You need fast-twitch athleticism, youthfulness. You need this generation of players who know velocity as a first language. You need rangy players on defense. The numbers bear out that younger players are the preferred way to go.
Players 30 and younger this year hit .247. Players in the 31-35 year-old demographic hit 10 points worse, .237, their worst showing ever. There was a time when front offices valued those 31-35 players because it seemed to be the peak intersection of experience and physical tools. Front offices were afraid to commit to younger players because of the lack of reps and track records. Those days are over.
The difference on the field in NLCS Game 3 was striking. The Brewers are the fastest team in baseball, as measured by sprint speed. The Dodgers are 24th.
The Brewers started a lineup and a pitcher with an average age of 26.1. They became the first team in history with a second postseason game starting three players 22 and younger: leftfielder Jackson Chourio, shortstop Cooper Pratt and rightfielder Luis Lara. Chourio opened the game with a first-pitch homer. Pratt smacked three hits, stole a base and scored a run. Lara flew around rightfield like a bird of prey, snaring anything that dared enter his airspace.
Watching Chourio, 22, Garrett Mitchell, 28, and Lara, 21, patrol the outfield was like watching an Olympic sprint relay team.
On the other side of the field, the Dodgers, especially their bats, looked old and slow. The average age of their starting 10 was 32.3 years old—more than six years older than Milwaukee’s fearless group. Only two starting Dodgers were in their 20s: centerfielder Andy Pages, 25, and Kyle Tucker, 29, who with his diminished range and baserunning has been trending older than his age.
By starting eight players 31 and older, these Dodgers joined the 2023 Dodgers, who got bounced by the Diamondbacks, as the only teams in the past 19 postseasons to trot out so many starting players that old in a game.
Fittingly, the old team played an outdated style of baseball, one from a generation ago. The ninth-place hitter, Tommy Edman, twice batted after the leadoff runner reached first base. Twice manager Dave Roberts did not ask him to bunt.
“I thought about it, but it’s just, he had a good pitch to hit. Flew out,” Roberts said. “I just didn’t feel giving up an out right there. Early in the game, I wanted Tommy to hit ...
“We haven’t been getting hits with runners in scoring position. To give up an out, to bank on getting a hit with runners in scoring position, I’d rather just try to maybe slug, hit a double.”
Edman was a below average hitter (97 OPS+) with a .385 slug this season.
Roberts and the Dodgers keep waiting for slug to show up at the expense of forfeiting the situational baseball as deployed by the other three remaining teams, the youthful Brewers, Guardians and Rays. The Dodgers still may be waiting Thanksgiving morning.
For instance, the Dodgers were down 1-0 in the sixth when Roberts sent 36-year-old Max Muncy to hit for Pages with runners on first and second and no outs. In that situation, the Brewers are bunting. Milwaukee plays get-em-over, get-em-in ball. The Dodgers? No way. Muncy is a three-true outcome guy. He is not going to bunt. Again, the Dodgers played for slug and got nothing. Muncy struck out. Will Smith, 31, did save the rally with a two-run double. But the Dodgers would go 1-for-12 after that against hard-throwing relievers D.L. Hall and Trevor Megill.
The lineup remained cold. Shohei Ohtani, 32, cannot pull a baseball because of lower-half injuries that won’t allow him to properly turn his hips and get to a firm front side. Freeman, 37, has three extra-base hits since Aug. 31.
“[Our] pitching staff has been great, to be honest,” Rojas said. “It’s really hard to put it into context when you have to pitch and have to play defense with a one run lead every single time. It’s like asking these guys to just throw a perfect inning every single time. It’s not sustainable. So, the blame is on the offense. We all know we could’ve done better, but nothing we can do now.”
How in the world has Milwaukee made Los Angeles look so bad?
“It’s pretty simple,” Muncy said. “We’ve played like [poop]. They’ve played great.”
Occam’s razor (or commode) aside, the one-sided NLCS is bigger than that. It stands as a changing of the guard, recalling the 1964 World Series, when the St. Louis Cardinals, emblematic of the National League embracing Black and Latin American players, ended the dynasty of an aging New York Yankees team, then the second oldest team in baseball. The younger, faster, harder-throwing, more creative team has been, beyond doubt, the better team.
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

item.title: [reviewingthebrew.com] Blake Snell’s pregame comments come back to bite him in most satisfying way for Brewers fans
item.dc:creator: Owen Jonas
item.description: "The way Pat [Murphy] talks and how he talks to the team is way different than last year...How do you counter that? How do you get them into a different place? I think they're in a good spot now, especially being up 2-0, but adversity hits, and that's when thoughts start racing." Those were Blake Snell's comments during his pre-start press conference on Tuesday afternoon before he took the mound for the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, as seen in the vide
item.content:encoded:
"The way Pat [Murphy] talks and how he talks to the team is way different than last year...How do you counter that? How do you get them into a different place? I think they're in a good spot now, especially being up 2-0, but adversity hits, and that's when thoughts start racing."
Those were Blake Snell's comments during his pre-start press conference on Tuesday afternoon before he took the mound for the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series, as seen in the video below. The two-time Cy Young Award winner, who dominated the Milwaukee Brewers in last year's NLCS, alluded to the fact that Pat Murphy's squad, which was among the most resilient in baseball this year, could spiral when faced with adversity. For a team that now has five come-from-behind wins in their first seven postseason games this year, those comments fell flat.
Not only were Snell's comments met with eye rolls from a Brewers fanbase that has watched their team face adversity head-on throughout the year, rather than shy away from it, but the Dodgers' southpaw's assessment of his opponent also came back to bite him during his Game 3 start.
Between Jackson Chourio's first-pitch, leadoff home run, and the start of the seventh inning last night, Snell looked virtually unhittable. He was locating all four of his pitches, generating a ton of whiffs, and keeping his team in the game despite his offense's lack of production. In the bottom of the sixth inning, however, that offense broke through, and the Dodgers took the lead. Said offense was mostly generated by Abner Uribe's lack of command, which led him to load the bases with three walks, but a big two-RBI double off the left-center wall from the struggling Will Smith was key to Los Angeles taking a one-run lead.
With just nine outs left to overcome that one-run deficit, it could easily be said that the Brewers were facing adversity. However, rather than let their "thoughts race," as Snell expected them to, Murphy's team, just as they've done throughout the postseason, immediately responded. In the top of the seventh, with Snell nearing the end of his outing, Andrew Vaughn led off the inning with a seven-pitch walk. Then, Jake Bauers turned in the at-bat of the postseason, by battling Snell for 10 pitches before crushing a go-ahead, two-run homer on the 11th offering from the Dodgers' southpaw. Immediately after that momentum-shifting swing, Snell missed his spot with a changeup to Garrett Mitchell, and the Brewers outfielder made him pay by crushing a solo homer to nearly the exact same spot that Bauers' home run landed.
In that regard, it wasn't the Brewers whose thoughts started racing when adversity struck, but rather it was Snell, who let the leadoff walk and the lengthy at-bat from Bauers derail what was otherwise an excellent start. The Brewers' social media team poked fun at this narrative switch with the post seen below.
Snell, however, took the high road after the game, and for that he should be commended. Rather than double down on his inaccurate assessment of the Brewers or make excuses for his lack of execution in the seventh inning, Snell congratulated his former teammate, Bauers, for what was truly an incredible at-bat and an unbelievable swing.
Blake Snell makes up for pregame comments with classy message about former teammate Jake Bauers in post-game interview
Back in 2018, Snell and Bauers played together on the Tampa Bay Rays. At the end of that season, Snell was named the AL Cy Young Award winner, and Bauers was traded to Cleveland after a lackluster rookie year. Fast forward eight years, and the two met in what was the biggest at-bat of the NLCS thus far.
After the game, Snell acknowledged the journey that Bauers has been on since they were teammates, saying, as seen in the video below, "I've seen all the ups and downs he's been through and it's been a lot of downs, so for him to go through this right now, he's earned it. Hats off to him."
On the specific at-bat, which was the second time Bauers has seen at least 11 pitches in an at-bat in the last two games, Snell said, "I mean what an at-bat. I mean I threw everything I had...This is the best I've ever seen him play."
It's a classy response from Snell, whose team now faces the reality of winning four straight games against the best team in baseball just to keep their season alive. Snell could have made excuses, but instead he decided to simply give Bauers the respect he deserves for what was one of, if not the most impressive at-bat of the postseason.
Following Snell's pregame comments, his post-game response and praise for Bauers undoubtedly represented a shift in the narrative. Whereas claiming the first sign of adversity could derail the Brewers' series lead didn't offer the necessary respect to the team and culture that has been built in Milwaukee, Snell's post-game interview was filled with respect for his opponent. When an opposing hitter puts together an at-bat like Bauers did in the seventh inning of Game 3, it's hard not to give them the respect they deserve.

item.title: [awfulannouncing.com] MLB on Fox crew can't stop picking against the Brewers
item.dc:creator: Matt Yoder
item.description: If you’ve been on any social media platform in October, you have likely learned quickly that Milwaukee Brewers fans aren’t happy with Fox Sports and its coverage of the 2026 MLB postseason. Every fanbase has an element that feels the national network broadcasts are against them; it doesn’t matter who. But Brewers fans are approaching the “us against the world” territory that’s usually only reserved for the lunatic fringe of Ohio State fans the way the postseason has been going. The biggest issue
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve been on any social media platform in October, you have likely learned quickly that Milwaukee Brewers fans aren’t happy with Fox Sports and its coverage of the 2026 MLB postseason.
Every fanbase has an element that feels the national network broadcasts are against them; it doesn’t matter who. But Brewers fans are approaching the “us against the world” territory that’s usually only reserved for the lunatic fringe of Ohio State fans the way the postseason has been going.
The biggest issue has been their belief that MLB on Fox lead announcer Joe Davis is biased against them because he is the voice of the Los Angeles Dodgers throughout the season. Look at any highlight or any call, and you’ll see Brewers fans picking apart Davis’ work like a biology exam. How much of that is real? How much of it is Davis’ health issues and not having the full strength of his voice? And how much of it is just being imagined? Your answer to that question probably depends on which state you reside in and your rooting interests in the series.
What isn’t imagined is the lack of deference shown to the Brewers at the studio desk, where David Ortiz, Alex Rodriguez, and Derek Jeter all picked the Dodgers to win Game 3 of the series before they got beat by Milwaukee to fall behind 0-3 in the National League Championship Series.
It’s prediction time for Game 3 of the NLCS!
@AROD: Dodgers 5-3
@davidortiz: Dodgers 5-3
@derekjeter: Dodgers 4-3
@MLBONFOX https://t.co/yWaYFQVTCd
— FOX Sports (@FOXSports) October 15, 2026
And if that wasn’t enough, two out of the three analysts also picked the Dodgers to win Game 2 back in Milwaukee with only Ortiz picking the Brewers to win either game.
It’s prediction time for Game 2 of the NLCS!
@AROD: Dodgers 2-1
@davidortiz: Brewers 3-1
@derekjeter: Dodgers 3-1
@MLBONFOX https://t.co/3tRqUyO9g5
— FOX Sports (@FOXSports) October 12, 2026
Joe Davis has had to battle accusations of Dodgers bias throughout his entire career. That’s bound to happen given his position and the success of the franchise, regardless of whether or not they’re actually based in reality. It sure didn’t seem like he was holding anything back when the Brewers went back-to-back off Blake Snell to pick up the win in Game 3 of the series. But it’s a much more natural disrespect card to play when the big-name analysts on set continue to pick against you, and you keep winning anyway.
Hopefully, at some point, Brewers fans will be able to enjoy what is close to a historic run to the World Series without worrying so much about the broadcasters.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Dodgers Reveal Lineup As They Aim to Extend Season Past Game 4
item.dc:creator: Aaron Coloma
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers set their lineup for their NLCS Game 4 matchup against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday. The Dodgers currently face a 3-0 deficit in the series, and need to win Thursday’s game to keep their World Series hopes alive. They managed just two runs in Game 3 of the NLCS, the first of three potential games in Los Angeles. Who is Pitching For the Dodgers? As they announced before the start of the series, the Dodgers have Tyler Glasnow on the mound for the fourth game of the NLC
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers set their lineup for their NLCS Game 4 matchup against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday.
The Dodgers currently face a 3-0 deficit in the series, and need to win Thursday’s game to keep their World Series hopes alive. They managed just two runs in Game 3 of the NLCS, the first of three potential games in Los Angeles.
Who is Pitching For the Dodgers?
As they announced before the start of the series, the Dodgers have Tyler Glasnow on the mound for the fourth game of the NLCS. Injuries cut Glasnow’s regular season short, allowing him to make just 22 starts while posting a 3.49 ERA, but he earned an all-important win for the team in Game 4 of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves.
He threw 4.2 innings while allowing just one earned run, though he allowed five walks in the process. The veteran right-hander will look to keep the Brewers off of the board to give the Dodgers some kind of advantage in Thursday’s game.
Who is in the Dodgers’ Lineup?
The Dodgers made just one substitution in their lineup from Game 3, but drastically changed the order in which their hitters appear. Shohei Ohtani returned to the top of the lineup as the Dodgers’ designated hitter, followed by shortstop Mookie Betts and first baseman Freddie Freeman. Catcher Will Smith, after his two-run double in Wednesday’s loss, returns to the cleanup spot for the Dodgers, and right fielder Kyle Tucker follows him to the plate.
Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez will bat sixth, and Miguel Rojas remains in the lineup, though as the second baseman for Game 4. Batting eighth is center fielder Andy Pages, and Kiké Hernandez steps in at third base to round out the lineup.
Dodgers’ Lineup vs. Braves
1. Shohei Ohtani, DH
2. Mookie Betts, SS
3. Freddie Freeman, 1B
4. Will Smith, C
5. Kyle Tucker, RF
6. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
7. Miguel Rojas, 2B
8. Andy Pages, CF
9. Kiké Hernandez, 3B
P. Tyler Glasnow, RHP.
When Does Thursday’s Game Start?
First pitch for Thursday’s game comes at 5:00 p.m. PT, moved up one hour from the original start time of 6:00 p.m. PT due to scheduling changes in the ALDS. The Dodgers will look to generate some offense and extend their season with a strong performance in Game 4.

item.title: [tsn.ca] Bauers’ relentless at-bat have Brewers on brink of World Series after contemplating retirement
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.description: LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jake Bauers’ new lease on life allows him to worry less and give more. Two seasons after he nearly quit baseball, Bauers has become a big hitter in the middle of the Milwaukee Brewers’ lineup — and he put his renewed focus on display in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Jake Bauers’ new lease on life allows him to worry less and give more.
Two seasons after he nearly quit baseball, Bauers has become a big hitter in the middle of the Milwaukee Brewers’ lineup — and he put his renewed focus on display in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series.
Bauers’ two-run homer on the 11th pitch of a seventh-inning at-bat against Los Angeles Dodgers left-hander Blake Snell gave Milwaukee the lead for good in a 6-2 victory Wednesday, putting the Brewers on the cusp of their first World Series since 1982.
“Incredible at-bat,” manager Pat Murphy said.
Bauers fouled off five two-strike pitches before turning on a 97 mph fastball and launching it 412 feet to right field.
“Super sick,” teammate Garrett Mitchell said. “I think that more just goes to show the type of player he is. It’s a selfless at-bat. He’s just trying to put the ball in play. He’s trying to move the guy over, and put an incredible swing on that. For me, being able to watch that on deck was awesome.”
Mitchell followed with a home run of his own to chase Snell and make it 4-2. Milwaukee has a 3-0 lead in the best-of-seven NLCS, with Game 4 at Los Angeles on Thursday.
Bauers was drafted in 2013 by the San Diego Padres out of Marina High School in Huntington Beach, located about 40 miles south of Dodger Stadium. After batting .202 for the New York Yankees in 2023, he was traded that November to Milwaukee — where he hit .199 in 2024.
Ready to hang up his spikes, Bauer changed his mind when his wife told him she was pregnant. Wanting to be a provider for his growing family, he put off retirement and maintained their health insurance.
Earlier this week, Bauers spoke eloquently about his wife and her sacrifice while raising two rambunctious children while he is away playing baseball.
Now, he’s making fans all over Milwaukee feel like little kids again.
“There’s a lot of people to credit, man,” Bauers said after Wednesday’s game. “I’ve played a lot of places. I’ve picked up knowledge from a lot of different people.
“I think what changed for me this year was I stopped caring about results. I started caring about competing. I started caring about being in the moment and getting out of my own way.”
All that showed up in Game 2 of the series when he worked a two-out walk to load the bases on the 12th pitch he saw from Dodgers ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto in the third inning. Christian Yelich followed with a two-run single for a 3-2 lead in a 7-4 victory, ending Yamamoto’s outing.
Bauers, who turned 31 last week, is in his third year with Milwaukee — his fifth team in seven major league seasons. The first baseman and corner outfielder led the Brewers with 26 home runs and an .874 OPS during the regular season.
“Jake got an opportunity, that’s what he got,” Murphy said. “He got an opportunity to contribute, and he kind of found his offensive approach. And he kind of found, like, I’m really talented, but this is what serves me best. It’s a growth in the game. He’s continued to grow.”
Patient and disciplined with a sharp eye at the plate, Bauers drew 94 walks and compiled a .389 on-base percentage this season. He also had 86 RBIs in 144 games, shattering his previous career highs across the board.
“I came into this year feeling like there was really only one person holding me back, and that was myself,” Bauers said. “So I think I just gave myself the space to believe that I could play — I could play in this league.”
___
See AP’s full MLB coverage here
Doug Padilla, The Associated Press

item.content:encoded:
For Los Angeles Dodgers prospect Josue De Paula, what was to be his professional breakthrough turned out to be his MLB debut on September 11, 2026, and the 21-year-old hugged his father, Josue De Paula Sr., who came from New York to Miami to see his son in the majors, before taking the field against the Miami Marlins at loanDepot park.
His grandmother, Sixtra Brito De Paula, was also on hand to celebrate the accomplishment. Their presence was a reminder of the family ties that helped De Paula go from a young baseball enthusiast to one of the Dodgers’ most highly regarded prospects. His journey was shaped by encouragement, Dominican family roots and decisions that helped him keep developing his talent.
Details on Josue De Paula’s MLB debut and family support
De Paula made his big league debut in the Dodgers’ 6-2 win over the Marlins. He batted seventh as the designated hitter, flying out in his first at-bat and later walking. His first appearance didn't produce a hit, but it was the start of his career at baseball's highest level.
The promotion was a surprise. De Paula was playing for the Double-A Tulsa Drillers and was called up directly to the majors, skipping Triple-A. The Dodgers added him to the roster while Shohei Ohtani was sidelined, giving the young outfielder a chance to get to the big-league roster.
How Josue De Paula’s father fueled his MLB dream
Josue De Paula Sr. has encouraged his son’s baseball aspirations since the time Josue De Paula Sr.’s son was 4 years old. The debut was particularly meaningful due to their shared connection to the sport. De Paula Sr. told MLB.com that it was an unforgettable moment that he was still processing emotionally. The hug between father and son before the game encapsulated the importance of years of support and anticipation.
The family’s baseball odyssey also included a major move during the COVID-19 pandemic. With schools closed in Brooklyn, De Paula moved to the Dominican Republic to stay with his uncles and keep training. He went to El Niche Baseball Academy in Santo Domingo before signing as an international amateur with the Dodgers in 2022. His father’s Dominican roots gave added significance to the young player’s progress.
Josue De Paula’s Dodgers rise followed family sacrifices
De Paula’s promotion came after a standout season for Tulsa. In 124 Double-A games in 2026, he hit .303 with 27 home runs, 104 RBIs and a.948 OPS. Those numbers helped make him one of the Dodgers’ most promising young hitters and supported the decision to bring him straight to the major leagues.
His grandmother, Sixtra Brito De Paula, has been an important link to Dominican culture and family. As a child, she recalled that he often carried a baseball bat, according to MLB.com. She also said she cooked traditional Dominican food during his visits and spent time with him.
Her memories hinted at the family life behind his professional success.
Josue De Paula’s debut marked a family milestone
Family members who had watched him develop long before the Dodgers promoted him shared in his first big league appearance. The debut was a personal milestone as well as a professional one, with his father's journey to Miami and his grandmother's presence there.
For the Dodgers, De Paula’s promotion presented an opportunity to evaluate a young hitter after his productive minor league season. For his family, it was the culmination of years of encouragement, training and patience, and his MLB journey is still developing, but his debut made it clear that his progress has been supported by more than just individual talent. Sixtra Brito De Paula and Josue De Paula Sr.'s presence proved how strong family still is in his path in baseball.

item.description: LOS ANGELES -- Patience and some unexpected power have the Milwaukee Brewers on the brink of their first World Series appearance in 44 years, and they will get their first chance to advance in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday. Jake Bauers turned an 11-pitch at-bat into a go-ahead two-run homer on Wednesday as the Brewers finished off a 6-2 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 3. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- Patience and some unexpected power have the Milwaukee Brewers on the brink of their first World Series appearance in 44 years, and they will get their first chance to advance in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday.
Jake Bauers turned an 11-pitch at-bat into a go-ahead two-run homer on Wednesday as the Brewers finished off a 6-2 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 3.
Milwaukee has a commanding 3-0 lead in the best-of-seven series entering the Thursday contest at Dodger Stadium.
Bauers' tenacity was so complete that on-deck hitter Garrett Mitchell went to the plate inspired. He added his own home run, giving a team that rarely used might this season its third home run of the game.
"Super sick," Mitchell said of the at-bat by Bauers. "He's trying to move the guy over, and (he) put an incredible swing on that. For me being able to watch that on deck was awesome."
The power display came after the Brewers hit 154 home runs in the regular season. Only the Toronto Blue Jays had fewer in the major leagues with 152.
"We play for each other," Bauers said. "When you have 26 guys that are bought into that and believe that and show up every day, completely selfless, playing for each other, it's a special thing to be a part of."
Milwaukee announced Thursday that rookie left-hander Shane Drohan will get the start as the team attempts to complete a sweep that would avenge their sweep at the hands of Los Angeles in last year's NLCS.
Advertisement
Drohan will be making his postseason debut. He was 7-5 with a 4.19 ERA and two saves in 33 games (19 starts) in the regular season. He faced the Dodgers three times (one start) and had no decisions with a 4.66 ERA, striking out 12 and walking five in 9 2/3 innings.
The Dodgers will put their season on the line with Tyler Glasnow on the mound. The right-hander started the Game 4 clincher in the NL Division Series against the Atlanta Braves and gave up one run over 4 2/3 innings but walked five.
In nine career regular-season appearances (five starts) against the Brewers, Glasnow is 0-3 with a 4.55 ERA. He also started Game 3 of the 2025 NLCS against Milwaukee and gave up one run over 5 2/3 innings in a no-decision.
While getting Glasnow to find his command will be key, the Dodgers also need some offensive consistency. Shohei Ohtani has struggled since late in the regular season and was moved to the No. 6 spot in the order for Game 3. He came through by reaching base three times, including a hard-hit single late in the game.
Los Angeles catcher Will Smith, who had been in a 1-for-25 postseason slide, delivered a two-run double. However, the Dodgers finished with just five hits on the night after collecting just three in their Game 2 loss at Milwaukee.
"I'll talk to them (Thursday)," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said of his players. "They know what's at stake. We've won four in a row a number of times this year. Ten times, I think, something like that."
And Roberts knows what a comeback from a 3-0 deficit in a league championship series looks like. His stolen base inspired the Boston Red Sox to an improbable rally over the New York Yankees in 2004. That was the only time in the previous 42 instances that a major league team escaped an 0-3 postseason hole to win a best-of-seven series.
"Our guys know how good (the Brewers) are. Our guys know what we're up against," Roberts said. "But that doesn't change anything. We come out and play the same way every time."
--Doug Padilla, Field Level Media
