item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Andy Pages single beats Braves, Dodgers win NLDS in 4 games
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: It took until the seventh inning of the fourth game of the National League Division Series for the Dodgers to get their first hit with a runner in scoring position. But Andy Pages made it count, with a two-run single to break a tie in a 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves on Wednesday night at Truist Park, clinching the NLCS to send the Dodgers to their third National League Championship Series in a row. The winning rally started with a single by Teoscar Hernández, just minutes after crashing into t
item.content:encoded:
It took until the seventh inning of the fourth game of the National League Division Series for the Dodgers to get their first hit with a runner in scoring position. But Andy Pages made it count, with a two-run single to break a tie in a 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves on Wednesday night at Truist Park, clinching the NLCS to send the Dodgers to their third National League Championship Series in a row.
The winning rally started with a single by Teoscar Hernández, just minutes after crashing into the left field wall on a Braves double in the previous half-inning. That ended the night for Tyler Mahle, who continued to have the Dodgers number, once again pitching into the seventh.
In came Game 2 Braves hero Didier Fuentes, whose second batter faced was fellow 21-year-old pinch-hitter Josue De Paula, only 24 days his senior. De Paula, in just his second postseason plate appearance, walked, then was removed for pinch-runner Tommy Edman. Kyle Tucker also walked to load the bases, setting up Pages — the Dodgers RBI leader this season — to single home a pair.
After going hitless in his first two games this series, Pages had two hits in Game 3 and two more in Game 4, equaling his total for the entire postseason in 2025. The hit also snapped an 0-for-14 skid by the Dodgers with runners in scoring position to start this series.
The first of those runs snapped a string of 22 straight innings by Mahle against the Dodgers without allowing an earned run, dating all the way back to 2022.
Edgardo Henriquez, who entered with one out in the sixth inning and stranded a runner on second, followed with a scoreless seventh inning to bookend the Dodgers rally, and earned the win.
Just like in Game 3, Tanner Scott pitched a scoreless eighth and Edwin Díaz closed out the win in the ninth, giving the Dodgers the planned back end of their bullpen that hadn't really been fully intact since early April.
Dodgers pitchers allowed eight total runs in the four-game series.
Max power
Max Muncy added some insurance with a solo home run in the ninth inning, extending his Dodgers career postseason record with now 19 home runs. Muncy also homered in Games 1 and 2 of this series, matching his most prolific postseason series with the long ball. He also hit three home runs in the 2019 NLDS against the Washington Nationals.
Sloppy start
Both teams exchanged mistakes for each other's first run, including an errant throw into center field on a stolen base attempt from each side. Michael Harris II got a great jump from third base on a wild pitch by Tyler Glasnow that didn't get too far from home plate in the first inning, catching the Dodgers flat-footed. In the top of the second, Shohei Ohtani walked, stole second and went to third on the bad throw, then scored when a Max Muncy popup into short left field was biffed by shortstop Mauricio Dubón.
Glasnow improved a bit as the game progressed, and didn't allow another hit after Harris led off the game with a single. But, like Blake Snell in Game 2, Glasnow on Wednesday walked five batters, including two in the fifth inning — a leadoff free pass to Austin Riley after getting ahead 0-2, and a two-out, four-pitch walk to Ronald Acuña Jr. to end Glasnow's night early.
The Dodgers right-hander struck out five with those five walks in his 4 2/3 innings, and like Snell limited the damage to only one run. Alex Vesia helped, inducing a groundout to second base to end the fifth inning with those two Glasnow walks left stranded on base, and the game still tied.
Glasnow threw 78 pitches, 44 for strikes.
Not so free passes
None of Glasnow's five walks in Game 4 scored, and none of the 18 Braves who walked in the NLDS have touched home plate. But there have still been costs to that Dodgers wildness. For one, the Dodgers had to turn to its bullpen much earlier than hoped in two of the four games.
Also, two of Snell's walks in the first inning of Game 2, pushing Acuña to third base, which allowed him to score on an infield single. In Game 3, the pinch-hit walk by Rowdy Tellez pushed Dubón to third base, which allowed him to score on a groundout. So the walks have been costly, even if not as much as perhaps they should have been.
NLDS Game 4 particulars
Home run: Max Muncy (3)
WP — Edgardo Henriquez (1-0): 1 2/3 IP, 1 hit
LP — Tyler Mahle (0-1): 6 1/3 IP, 3 hits, 2 runs (1 earned), 1 walk, 4 strikeouts
Sv — Edwin Díaz (2): 1 IP, 1 strikeout
Up next
The Dodgers move on to a third consecutive National League Championship Series, and eighth in the last 11 years, beginning Sunday night (time TBD, Fox Sports) either in Milwaukee against the Brewers or at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles against the Padres.

item.title: [CBS Sports] 2026 MLB playoffs: Winners and losers as Andy Pages gets redemption as Dodgers advance, Guardians stay alive
item.dc:creator: Matt Snyder
item.description: MLB's postseason continued on Wednesday with four potential Division Series clinchers. Regardless of the outcomes, this will be the last day with four games this season, so enjoy it. We won't get more than two games per day moving forward. In the National League, the Los Angeles Dodgers sent the Atlanta Braves home for good with their Game 4 win to advance to the NLCS, and the Milwaukee Brewers are trying to close out their series against the San Diego Padres. On the American League side, the Ch
item.content:encoded:
MLB's postseason continued on Wednesday with four potential Division Series clinchers. Regardless of the outcomes, this will be the last day with four games this season, so enjoy it. We won't get more than two games per day moving forward.
In the National League, the Los Angeles Dodgers sent the Atlanta Braves home for good with their Game 4 win to advance to the NLCS, and the Milwaukee Brewers are trying to close out their series against the San Diego Padres. On the American League side, the Chicago White Sox suffered their first loss of the playoffs as the Cleveland Guardians staved off elimination, while the Tampa Bay Rays are trying to finish a three-game sweep over the New York Yankees.
Here are the final scores and schedule for Wednesday's postseason action:
- FINAL: Guardians 9, White Sox 3 (box score); White Sox lead series 2-1
- FINAL: Dodgers 4, Braves 1 (box score); Dodgers win series 3-1
- LIVE: Rays at Yankees (GameTracker); Rays lead series 2-0
- UPCOMING: Brewers at Padres (GameTracker); Brewers lead series 2-1
To sum up all the Division Series action, we're here to declare a winner and loser from each of the four Wednesday contests. You can find those declarations just below.
Winner: Andy Pages
One of the Dodgers' worst playoff hitters came through with redemption
Believe it or not, the Dodgers entered Game 4 of the NLDS having only scored runs on home runs thus far in the series. Seven home runs had brought home 10 Dodgers runs, and that was enough to give them a 2-1 lead in the best-of-five series. They had gone 0 for 13 with runners in scoring position.
An error scored them a run early in Game 4, but they still hadn't gotten a clutch hit without muscling up for big-time power.
Fast-forward to the top of the seventh inning. It was a 1-1 game. Braves reliever Didier Fuentes came on with a runner on and two outs. He got a groundout before he walked two Dodgers hitters and manager Walt Weiss decided to turn to the veteran Robert Suarez with the bases loaded and two out. Andy Pages was coming to the plate.
Pages came through with a line-drive single up the middle to plate two runs.
Not only was it the knock that ended up sending the Dodgers back to the NLCS, but it was a bit of playoff redemption for Pages. He was so bad at the plate last year in the playoffs that the Dodgers elected to remove him from the starting lineup for Games 6 and 7 of the World Series after previously starting him every game. Heading into Game 4 on Wednesday, Pages was a career .123/.165/.210 hitter in the playoffs.
Loser: Braves situational hitting
The Braves went 1 for 23 in the series with RISP
Thanks particularly to five walks issued by Dodgers starting pitcher Tyler Glasnow, the Braves had their share of chances to score runs in Game 4. They just couldn't come through in the clutch the way Pages did for the Dodgers. Well, that and they also had some rough batted-ball luck.
A leadoff Ozzie Albies double in the sixth inning didn't amount to any runs. Per Statcast, that double, by the way, would've been a home run in 29 of the 30 MLB ballparks. It's just that they happened to be playing in the one where it didn't leave the yard. Then Mauricio Dubón sent a two-out liner to right field that hung up just long enough for Kyle Tucker to catch it. The expected batting average there was .620.
They also failed, though. Plenty in the entire series. In Game 1, they were 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position. In Game 2, despite the win, the Braves left 11 men on base. In Game 3, they were 0 for 6 with runners in scoring position, leaving six more on base.
In Game 4? Yep, that would be 0 for 7 with seven left on.
In all, that's 1 for 23 with runners in scoring position in the four-game series with 28 runners left on.
Part of this is a function of facing great playoff pitching against a defense that is always very well-positioned. Part of it is simply bad luck in where the balls are hit hard. Part of it is a failure in execution.
Taking splits like RISP stats isn't a predictive measure or anything like that, but it can tell the story in a series like this. In the case of the Dodgers taking the Braves out, we got here in large part due to the Braves leaving a high school classroom's worth of runners on base.
Winner: Jo Adell
The Guardians acquired Adell in front of the trade deadline and he's been an RBI machine
As the trade deadline came into focus, the Guardians, looking for cheap help on offense, ended up grabbing outfielder Jo Adell from the Angels in exchange for Double-A catcher Jacob Cozart. In 48 games for Cleveland, Adell posted a 108 OPS+ and drove home 32 runs. In Game 2, he recorded an eighth-inning RBI triple that nearly left the yard.
In Game 3 on Wednesday in Game 3, he came to the plate with two outs, bases loaded and a tied 1-1 score. Adell came through in a big way.
Just like that, it was a 4-1 Guardians lead. Adell also became the 16th player in postseason history to triple in back-to-back games (via Sarah Langs).
Adell's three-RBI triple moved the Guardians' chances to win the game from 52.8% to 78.8%. This was the largest difference-maker in the game, and a monster shift at that.
Loser: White Sox's missed opportunities
The White Sox had plenty of chances for crooked numbers in this one
Playing in front of an electric crowd, ready to clinch a postseason series at home for the first time since 1906 (and we all remember that one, right?), the White Sox had several chances to put up a crooked number and weren't able to come through.
- In the first, Sam Anonacci walked and Miguel Vargas singled to give them two runners with no outs. Kyle Teel came through with a one-out double, but Vargas was held at third. Chase Meidroth and Tristan Peters struck out to leave two on base.
- Meidroth and Peters started the fourth with consecutive doubles, but the following three hitters were retired, so, again, the White Sox settled for just the one run.
- In the fifth, Antonacci singled and Vargas walked. The runners moved up on a grounder and then Teel ripped a line drive toward right field, only to watch it get snared by Guardians second baseman Travis Bazzana, who then doubled Vargas off second. The expected batting average on this one makes it even tougher to swallow for the White Sox faithful, as it was .940. This means that 94% of the time a ball hit with that exit velocity at that launch angle ends up as a hit. This was one of the 6% that found a glove.
- In the sixth, with two outs, Braden Montgomery walked, Randal Grichuk singled, Colson Montgomery was hit by a pitch and then so was Antonacci. They got a run, but the bases were loaded for their best player, Vargas. He hit a rocket toward left, but Guardians third baseman José Ramírez was able to knock the ball down and get Vargas at first. Vargas hit it hard, with a .580 expected batting average. It just didn't work out.
You never want to come away empty-handed in those innings, and the White Sox were able to get a single run in three of those frames. Still, it feels like there was a lot left on the board here from the home team. An explosion in a single inning could've demoralized the Guardians and ultimately sent them home. Some of the issues were their own fault, and some were bad luck. It all added up to a Game 4 White Sox loss.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Teoscar Hernández Believes Looks at Atlanta Bullpen Will Help
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers leave Los Angeles tied 1-1 in the NLDS, but Teoscar Hernández believes the first two games may still help them as the series shifts to Atlanta. The Braves have already shown the Dodgers a lot of their bullpen, and Hernández thinks that can matter when the same arms start showing up again in Games 3 and 4. With Chris Sale waiting for them Tuesday, the Dodgers will need every edge they can get. A Better Read on Atlanta’s Bullpen “I think so,” Hernández said when asked
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers leave Los Angeles tied 1-1 in the NLDS, but Teoscar Hernández believes the first two games may still help them as the series shifts to Atlanta.
The Braves have already shown the Dodgers a lot of their bullpen, and Hernández thinks that can matter when the same arms start showing up again in Games 3 and 4. With Chris Sale waiting for them Tuesday, the Dodgers will need every edge they can get.
A Better Read on Atlanta’s Bullpen
“I think so,” Hernández said when asked whether seeing so many Atlanta relievers could help later in the series. “Moving forward, now that we’ve seen basically the best out of the bullpen, we can have a better plan. We can make a better plan for Tuesday and Wednesday.”
Atlanta leaned heavily on its bullpen in Game 2 and found a way to hold the Dodgers to one run. Hernández said the Dodgers will take what they learned from those matchups and use it when they see those pitchers again.
He also brushed aside the idea that Sunday felt like a major missed chance because of the number of pitchers Atlanta had already used during the Wild Card round.
“Not really,” he said. “We didn’t think about it. We were just trying to make the best plan that we could get for the series and trying to execute whatever we have to do.”
Experience Matters Now
With the series down to three games, Hernández pointed to the Dodgers’ recent postseason experience as something they can draw on.
“I think it’s big,” he said. “We’ve been in tougher spots than this one. It’s a one-one series.
“We all know they’re going to have the best starting pitcher that they have in Sale. We’re just going to try to be ready, go with the best plan and try to execute it.”
The Dodgers will counter Sale with Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
“It’s good,” Hernández said. “That’s the best pitcher that we have going against the best pitcher that they have. It’s going to be a good matchup, a good game.
“Hopefully at the end of the day, we get the win.”
Getting the Offense Going
The Dodgers have relied almost entirely on home runs for their scoring through the first two games, and Hernández said the answer is tied to better at-bats and strike-zone control.
“It’s just having good at-bats, not swinging at bad pitches,” he said. “Like I was saying, they were executing really good pitches today. They didn’t give us a really good chance to score runs.”
Hernández felt the Dodgers stayed patient Sunday.
“Yeah, I feel so,” he said. “Like I said, they made some good pitches, borderline pitches. It’s one of those days.”
Even with runners reaching throughout the game, Hernández said the approach in the dugout stayed the same.
“Just go in there, fight every at-bat, every pitch, and try to get a good result at the end of the day.”
The Dodgers will get another look at Atlanta’s pitching Tuesday. This time, Sale will be the first challenge. After that, Hernández believes the familiarity gained over the first two games could start working in their favor.

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.dc:creator: SANKEI DIGITAL INC
item.description: ナ・リーグ地区シリーズ第4戦（ブレーブス－ドジャース、7日、アトランタ）米大リーグ、ドジャースのエンリケ・ヘルナンデス内野手（34）が地区シリーズ第4戦前の会見に登壇し、第3戦で先発した山本由伸投手（28）にマウンドでかけた「汚い言葉」を明かした。 第3戦の五回は山本が1死満塁のピンチを背負うと、捕手のスミスと三塁のE・ヘルナンデスが右腕に声をかけた。山本はその言葉を「すごく汚い言葉でした」と苦笑いを浮かべるも、「すごく励まされました」と明かしていた。 キケは「これはお前の試合だ。誰もブルペンで準備していない。これはお前の試合なんだ。お前を信頼している。これまでも切り抜けてきたし、今回も必ず切り抜けられると分かっている。自分にプレッシャーをかけすぎず、そのまま行け」と背中を押す言葉を投げかけたという。 さらに山本は米国の汚い言葉も知っているかという問いに「彼はアメリカ語を話すよ。アメリカ語だ」と報道陣の笑いを誘い、「これまで一緒にプレーしてきた中でも最も頭のいい選手の一人。彼は野球に対して注ぐのと同じくらいの努力と熱意を、英語の勉強にも注いでいる。試合の前にも後にも英語の授業を受けてい
item.content:encoded:
ナ・リーグ地区シリーズ第4戦（ブレーブス－ドジャース、7日、アトランタ）米大リーグ、ドジャースのエンリケ・ヘルナンデス内野手（34）が地区シリーズ第4戦前の会見に登壇し、第3戦で先発した山本由伸投手（28）にマウンドでかけた「汚い言葉」を明かした。
第3戦の五回は山本が1死満塁のピンチを背負うと、捕手のスミスと三塁のE・ヘルナンデスが右腕に声をかけた。山本はその言葉を「すごく汚い言葉でした」と苦笑いを浮かべるも、「すごく励まされました」と明かしていた。
キケは「これはお前の試合だ。誰もブルペンで準備していない。これはお前の試合なんだ。お前を信頼している。これまでも切り抜けてきたし、今回も必ず切り抜けられると分かっている。自分にプレッシャーをかけすぎず、そのまま行け」と背中を押す言葉を投げかけたという。
さらに山本は米国の汚い言葉も知っているかという問いに「彼はアメリカ語を話すよ。アメリカ語だ」と報道陣の笑いを誘い、「これまで一緒にプレーしてきた中でも最も頭のいい選手の一人。彼は野球に対して注ぐのと同じくらいの努力と熱意を、英語の勉強にも注いでいる。試合の前にも後にも英語の授業を受けている。誰も見ていないところでも、家に帰って英語のレッスンを受けている。今ではほとんど普通に会話できる。時にはGoogle翻訳が必要になることもあるが、ちゃんと会話が成立するよ」と影の努力まで明かした。

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers star Mookie Betts' birthday feat making MLB history proves he's a true champion appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
On Wednesday evening, the Los Angeles Dodgers will look to turn out the lights on the Atlanta Braves when the two teams hit the field for Game 4 of their NLDS matchup. The Dodgers climbed back into the driver's seat in this series on Tuesday in a Game 3 win thanks to an epic performance from pitcher Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
It's been a relatively quiet postseason thus far for Dodgers leadoff hitter Mookie Betts, but perhaps a personal milestone on Wednesday could help change that.
"Today is Mookie Betts' birthday. Birthdays are important. This will be the fourth time he plays a postseason game on his birthday, most in MLB history," reported Sarah Langs of the MLB on X, formerly Twitter.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Indeed, having a birthday in October means that Betts is no stranger to playing postseason baseball on the special occasion. He turns 34 years old on Wednesday, and has looked like an aging star for most of the series so far against the Braves, not making much happen at the plate.
However, on Wednesday, the Dodgers found a way to get to Braves ace Chris Sale thanks to two straight homers, the second of which was launched by former Atlanta star Freddie Freeman, to put three runs on the board, which was all they needed to get the comfortable win.
The Dodgers now sit just one win away from the NLCS, where they would play either the San Diego Padres or Milwaukee Brewers for the right to go to the World Series.
In any case, Game 4 of Braves vs Dodgers is set to get underway on Wednesday at 6:00 pm ET from Atlanta.
Related: Dodgers' Miguel Rojas not available for Game 4 of NLDS vs. Braves

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers recalled left-hander Justin Wrobleski to start in Friday's series opener on the road against the St. Louis Cardinals.
In a corresponding move, right-hander Landon Knack was optioned to Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Wrobleski, 24, was 1-1 with an 8.00 ERA in two appearances (one start) with Los Angeles earlier this season. Still considered a rookie, he was 1-2 with a 5.70 ERA in eight games (six starts) last season.
The Dodgers have been in scramble mode with injuries throughout their pitching staff, including three starters from their Opening Day pitching staff who are out with shoulder issues: Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow and Roki Sasaki.
Knack, 27, is 3-2 with a 5.12 ERA in nine appearances (seven starts). In Thursday's start against the New York Mets, he issued a career-high five walks and tied a career high with three home runs allowed.

item.title: [Rising Apple] Qualifying offer penalty can quickly eliminate NY Mets' Tarik Skubal backup plan
item.dc:creator: Tim Boyle

item.content:encoded:
I Stand Alone was a 2002 song by the rock band Godsmack featured in the film The Scorpion King. The song hardly stands alone as their lone hit or even above some of their lesser remembered releases. In MLB free agency, it’s Tarik Skubal who stands alone as the best of the bunch this offseason both from a pitching and hitting perspective. His market will be limited to the Los Angeles Dodgers, New York Mets, and maybe a mystery team thrown in.
Alternatives you ask? They aren’t good, Bob. One of the most realistic is Trevor Rogers. He was someone the Mets tried to trade for at the 2024 deadline only to come up short as he went from the Miami Marlins to the Baltimore Orioles instead. Terrible for Baltimore down the stretch, brilliant in an abbreviated 2025, and more average with signs of excellence in 2026, he’s a guy we should definitely believe fits the model of how David Stearns operates.
Rogers turns 29 this November. For him, coming off of a 10-11, 4.01 ERA season means seeking out an opportunity to maybe have an amazing 2027 and/or 2028 and re-enter free agency still young enough to get one of those fat contracts.
If Trevor Rogers receives a qualifying offer and rejects it, the Mets have to think twice about signing him
The QO was pretty much made for players like Rogers. He had a good, not great year. His 101 ERA+ suggests he was a fraction better than average.
However you want to rate him, it’s a little icky to think about giving up two draft picks to sign him. The Mets will, yet again, lose draft pick compensation for signing a QO rejector. The Mets lost $1 million in international bonus slot money plus their second and fifth highest draft picks last offseason when they inked Bo Bichette. Those same penalties should apply again this offseason if they choose to take the leap.
There are players where draft picks don’t matter. Juan Soto cost the Mets two picks and the international bonus slot money. Nobody argued. Eve Bichette felt worth it in some ways especially with the Mets already gaining a selection when Edwin Diaz departed.
Rogers seems a sure bet to decline the qualifying offer. He can guarantee himself more than what it’s worth and with additional years of control. Some health issues in his career will always have a pitcher in free agency looking for a way to capitalize and protect in case of another injury.
Not as expensive as Skubal yet costly to those of us who still haven’t adjusted baseball salaries for inflation, Rogers will find a way to guarantee himself around $50 million over two years plus additional seasons. He’s the kind of guy you sign for what you believe he will do and not what he has already accomplished. It’s not all that different from Zack Wheeler. During his time with the Mets, he was no ace but very good at times. The Philadelphia Phillies believed in the future enough. Will the Mets do so with Rogers?
Stearns hasn’t been hesitant to give out deals like this with inferior players. Frankie Montas getting a $17 million deal for 2025 plus the player option for 2026 never sat well with fans. Sean Manaea, Clay Holmes, and even Pete Alonso were all signed for short contracts with a player option. Oh, and Bichette, too. Even Soto has a chance to opt out with the creative pushback where the Mets can increase his salary to avoid him leaving.
Rogers is a part of the Plan-B package if the Mets miss on Skubal. Is it satisfactory enough? Plan-B requires one other addition. Rogers has had flashes of being awesome while the overall results have been more “meh.” That has been the M.O. under Stearns and whether we like it or not, he feels destined to become a hot Mets rumor this winter.
The qualifying offer penalty, perhaps, becomes too rich when the team can just as easily pivot to others who won’t have the same punishment following them around. The big irony is that because Skubal was traded mid-season he wouldn't cost the Mets anything more than cash. With Rogers, there's an added cost.

item.title: [The Atlanta Journal-Constitution] The Win Column: Is Freddie Freeman now an Atlanta villain?
item.dc:creator: Ken Sugiura
item.description: Greetings, Tyler Estep enthusiasts! You’ll be pleased to know that the admired and capable Tyler will be back next week. item.content:encoded:
Greetings, Tyler Estep enthusiasts!
You’ll be pleased to know that the admired and capable Tyler will be back next week. This will be my second and final missive in his estimable place.
But enough blathering. On with the newsletter. I apologize in advance that I’m not as concise as Tyler, but I make up for it in by being less funny.
HOW ARE WE FEELING ABOUT FREDDIE FREEMAN?
If you watched Tuesday’s broadcast of Game 3 of the NLDS between the Braves and the Dodgers or were at Truist Park, surely you heard the boos raining down on the longtime Brave when he came to the plate.
I was fascinated by this. On social media — granted, not the best barometer for anything except for measuring people’s capacity for surliness to complete strangers — there was a lot of chatter from fans about how Freeman cannot be welcomed back like the prodigal son, as has been the case since he signed with the Dodgers before the 2022 season.
At least not in the playoffs, his first at Truist in Dodgers colors.
It was a reasonable (and evidently popular) position to take, although I don’t know why there has to be a group think about this.
But the interesting thing to me was that the response went all the other way, to where he was getting booed with more intensity than anyone except maybe Shohei Ohtani.
I had thought the switch would just be from applause to indifference.
But it was like he went from “guy we still love” to “guy we now despise.”
It was almost like a scene out of a movie, where the boy has a dog he can no longer keep as a pet but the dog still follows him around so the boy tearfully has to turn on the dog (“Now, git! You hear me!”) to make it clear that he is no longer wanted. (That was weirdly specific, I realize.)
Was it because he left the Braves or because he’s one of the Dodgers’ best players (he did homer) or my own movie/dog/boy interpretation?
This was Freeman’s explanation, as reported in a story worth reading by colleague and longtime Freeman chronicler Gabe Burns:
“I’ve got a gray uniform on, I expect boos.”
Eager to hear your thoughts.
A DREAM SCENARIO
You may have missed this, but the Dream made a rather newsy announcement Tuesday. They will play all of their home games at State Farm Arena next season (and at least the one following) after playing for the past six seasons at Gateway Center Arena (capacity: 3,575, smallest in the WNBA).
The Dream liked the College Park arena but it was too small to be sustainable. But another aspect of it was, as much as they liked bragging about selling out Gateway Center, it was difficult to ascertain what the demand would be in a larger arena.
Ever since the team’s inception in 2008, they’ve had trouble drawing, even when they’ve had competitive teams, starting at State Farm (then Philips Arena).
But a telling moment came when the Dream played at State Farm in June against a non-marquee opponent (the Toronto Tempo) on a Monday night. In recent seasons, they’ve moved games to State Farm for surefire draws like Caitlyn Clark’s Indiana Fever and the Las Vegas Aces.
Team president and chief operating officer Morgan Shaw Parker told me then that “this is a way for us to really test that out and understand the market a little better. Because you can’t just understand if you’re only bringing in one (visiting) team to play (in State Farm).”
The Dream-Tempo game drew nearly 10,000.
That and other indicators evidently informed the ownership group that it was time to take the next step. It’s great for fans of the team and women’s basketball in general.
A team spokesperson told me Tuesday that it’s not yet decided if they’ll use a smaller configuration as they did for Game 1 of the WNBA semifinals on Sunday or use the full configuration.
It wouldn’t surprise me if it was a mixture. And the team’s ownership continues to explore having its own arena. (Georgia State Convocation Center makes a lot of sense to me.)
The Dream and New York Liberty play Game 2 of their WNBA semifinal series Wednesday night at State Farm. They are using the smaller configuration (closing off most of the upper deck) because of, I was told, the quick turnaround for playoff ticket sales.
Game 1 drew 9,745 and the get-in price for Game 2 on Seatgeek on Wednesday morning was $98.
A new chapter is beginning.
KIRBY SMART ASKED, WE ANSWERED
This is something of an homage to the very capable Tyler, whose work I really appreciate for the way he approaches sports. Saturday, after Georgia whipped up on Vanderbilt, Bulldogs coach Kirby Smart was asked about a particular officiating call on quarterback Gunner Stockton.
Smart declined to offer his evaluation of the call, saying “the last thing I do is judge officials,” which, if you’ve ever seen a Georgia game or are an SEC official, you may quibble with.
But he went on to explain his non-judging stance by saying he doesn’t even know — for instance, when a punt is shanked out of bounds — how officials determine where to spot the ball.
I saw that and thought: A) I am always intrigued by how Smart’s mind works, and B) This is prime Win Column material.
And so I sought out an answer.
Big thanks to former longtime SEC official Gus Morris, who delivered perfectly.
Per Morris (whose “Saturdays in the South” book about his life as an SEC official is great): “The referee is positioned near the punter and then, after the ball is punted away, goes to the punter’s spot. If the ball is punted out of bounds, he notes where it landed to establish the flight path of the ball.”
An official lined up deep downfield on the sideline (there’s one on each) starts to move up toward the line of scrimmage with an eye on the referee. (Not that important, but this “Where’s he going to stop?” march has always made me think of the mountain-climber game on “The Price is Right.” If you know, you know.)
“When he intersects with the line that the referee establishes, then you’ll see the referee (drop his raised arm) and then the deep-wing official will stop there and establish the spot there,” Morris told me. “It’s not just arbitrarily determined. There’s actually a mechanic that handles that situation.”
I thought that was pretty interesting. Hope you did, too.
At the Win Column, we are all Kirby Smart.
A SHOUTOUT TO MY DAD
To my chagrin, I will miss the remainder of the Braves NLDS and the Georgia-Alabama game because I will be off from this afternoon through Sunday for a great reason. My father, Go Sugiura, is turning 90 on Sunday and my family will be flying to San Francisco to help celebrate.
Among many other things, my dad fostered my love for sports and helped me on my path to this job. He gave me countless weekend afternoons in our backyard in Northfield, Illinois, playing catch and throwing batting practice in the spring and summer and tossing the football in the fall. I didn’t realize it then, but those were truly some of the best days of my life.
Serendipitously, he was able to get two Bears season tickets for the 1984 and 1985 seasons, the latter proving to be only arguably the greatest in NFL history, and we went to nearly all of them together. (Amusingly, my dad’s friend who gave up the tickets for those two years because the Bears had forever been mediocre wanted them back after that and then they didn’t go to another Super Bowl for almost 20 years.)
And while my dad knew little about the newspaper business and had no connections to leverage, he did what he could.
When I was in college, rather randomly, he ended up sharing an office floor with Walter Payton and, surely knowing he couldn’t ask for too many favors, spent one of them asking him if he could talk with me and share advice about journalism from his perspective as a former professional athlete. (Which Payton graciously did, and I still think back to.)
I went to Japan (my parents’ country of origin) after I graduated to study and travel (a trip my parents funded) and, as I began to look for a job upon my return, heard from The Philadelphia Inquirer.
I went to Philadelphia for an interview and when I met with an editor, she mentioned talking to my dad (because I’d left our home phone as my contact information) and smilingly referred to him as “your agent,” which I’m sure meant that he, as is his way, had been responsive, thorough and eager in his communication.
I didn’t get a job there immediately, and as I looked for a job after returning home, I remember he bought a CD-ROM (this was 1995) with the address of, literally, every publication in the United States.
Even, like, Cat Fancy magazine.
And his plan was that I was going to write to all of them to find a job. He set up a mail merge and the address labels and everything.
Thankfully, we didn’t follow through completely on this strategy, as it may have resulted in me becoming the unwitting cub reporter of Crocheting Monthly or some such.
Regardless, it was an expression of love that I cherish still.
Happy birthday, Dad. And thank you.
PHOTO OF THE DAY
Thanks for reading to the very bottom of the Win Column. Questions, comments, ideas? Contact me at tyler.estep@ajc.com (or me, Ken, at ken.sugiura@ajc.com)
Until next time.
Ken Sugiura is a sports columnist at the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. Formerly the Georgia Tech beat reporter, Sugiura started at the AJC in 1998 and has covered a variety of beats, mostly within sports.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- A race to first based turned into a violent collision that sent two players sprawling onto the field and, eventually, into the dugout.
Arizona's Ildemaro Vargas and the Los Angeles Dodgers' Max Muncy are sore but otherwise OK, but, boy, what a jolt.
"It was terrible," Diamondbacks second baseman Ketel Marte said through an interpreter after hitting a walk-off homer in Arizona's 3-2 win over Los Angeles on Thursday night. "In my 10 years, I've never seen a collision like that."
It came in the fifth inning when Muncy hit a ground ball down the line over first base.
Vargas fielded the ball behind the bag, spun around and, seeing pitcher Ryne Nelson wasn't covering, took off running, hoping to beat Muncy.
He didn't and the full-speed collision sent both players flying in the air, landing with a thud on opposite sides of the base.
A hush fell over the crowd as both players writhed in the dirt and trainers from both teams rushed out. Vargas and Muncy were on the field for several minutes before slowly making their way to their respective dugouts.
"Those are the types of things that you see on the baseball field when two players are lying on the dirt after trying to make a hustle play," Diamondbacks manager Torey Lovullo said. "It's tough to see, but they both got off the field."
Muncy left with shortness of breath and was being evaluated for a concussion. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said he wouldn't play Friday against the Angels -- it was already a scheduled day off -- but could be available over the weekend.
Muncy told reporters he was a little banged up but will be all right.
"I really hope Vargas is OK -- I sent something over to him," he said. "I'm hoping he's doing all right and he's not too bad. But just bad situation that looks like neither of us knew which direction to go."
Vargas sustained bruises down his left side -- thigh, ribs and neck. X-rays were negative and he told Lovullo he would be ready to play Friday, if needed.
"My whole body feels like I ran into a truck, but thankfully all the exams and tests were negative," Vargas said through an interpreter.
It could have been much worse.br/]

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers are back in Atlanta for Game 4 of the NLDS on Wednesday, needing just one more win to clinch the series. After getting to Chris Sale in Game 3, the Dodgers will face right-hander Tyler Mahle, who has turned heads since being acquired at the trade deadline from the San Francisco Giants.
After batting fifth in the starting lineup for the first time as a Dodger, Shohei Ohtani will once again be hitting in the middle third of the order, this time moving up to the cleanup spot with Teoscar Hernández sliding down to the fifth spot in the order.
Max Muncy makes his first start this series since batting 8th in Game 1 against left-hander Dylan Dodd, this time batting sixth in the lineup with Miguel Rojas getting the day off after dealing with back tightness. The hero of Game 3 on offense, Kiké Hernández, makes his second straight start, this time batting seventh while getting the start at second base. Kyle Tucker once again hits in the 8 spot while Andy Pages rounds things out after a multi-hit performance.
Runs have been hard to come by so far this series, as the Dodgers have plated just 10 combined runs over their first three postseason games, all of which have come via home runs. The main Achilles heel for the Dodgers has been their consistent inability to produce with runners in scoring position, as the team is 0-13 in those situations. The Braves, to their credit, have managed to get one hit with runners in scoring position, albeit across 14 at-bats, and have combined to score just eight runs over the first three games.
The Dodgers have fared well in previous matchups against Mahle, as the right-hander has a combined 3-3 record with a 3.15 ERA. Most of the damage came when Mahle was still with the Cincinnati Reds, and in his most recent start against the Dodgers back when he was with San Francisco, he shut them down over seven shutout innings in a 3-0 Giants win on April 22. Since joining Atlanta, Mahle finished the regular season with a 1.99 ERA and limited the Philadelphia Phillies to just one run in his most recent Wild Card start.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are coming off a massive Game 3 victory over the Atlanta Braves on the road at Truist Park on Tuesday night.
They’ll now take a 2-1 series lead into Wednesday’s matchup and sit just one win away from advancing to the NLCS as they continue to chase a third consecutive World Series title.
Ahead of the matchup. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts elected to make some changes to his starting lineup for the second straight day.
Dodgers Announce Teoscar Hernandez Change
Among those moving in the order is slugger Teoscar Hernandez, who hit third in the lineup Tuesday and will now drop to sixth for Game 4.
Hernandez is coming off back-to-back 0-for-4 performances. And Roberts will move catcher Will Smith into the No. 3 spot, while Shohei Ohtani moves from fifth to fourth and will bat cleanup.
Max Muncy will bat fifth in the lineup after starting Tuesday’s game on the bench.
Here’s the Dodgers starting lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: “Dodgers 10/7 M. Betts SS F. Freeman 1B W. Smith C S. Ohtani DH T. Hernández LF M. Muncy 3B E. Hernández 2B K. Tucker RF A. Pages CF T. Glasnow SP.”
Dodgers 10/7
M. Betts SS

W. Smith C
S. Ohtani DH
T. Hernández LF
M. Muncy 3B
E. Hernández 2B
K. Tucker RF
A. Pages CF
T. Glasnow SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) October 7, 2026
Looking at the Dodgers
L.A. has relied heavily on the long ball for its offense so far in this series against Atlanta.
After winning 5-3 in Game 1, losing 3-2 in Game 2 on Sunday and then winning 3-1 on Tuesday, all 10 of their combined runs in the series have come via home runs.
And they’ve seemingly done it with Shohei Ohtani being pretty much a non-factor at the plate.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Mets are watching the MLB playoffs from the sidelines after a disappointing 2026 campaign.
However, it’s important to keep tabs on former Mets who are having a profound impact on their new team.
One of those players is reliever Edwin Diaz, who is thriving with the Dodgers so far in the playoffs.
New York Mets fans know Diaz quite well, as he spent six seasons in Queens and was named to two All-Star appearances with the Metropolitans.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Face Major Tyler Mahle Decision After MLB Playoffs
Edwin Diaz Finding Success with Dodgers in MLB Playoffs
Edwin Diaz has had a rocky season after signing a massive contract extension with the Los Angeles Dodgers, but it seems he’s starting to find his footing in recent outings, which included a save in Game Three of the NLDS on Tuesday against the Atlanta Braves.
In the 2026 MLB playoffs, Diaz has allowed zero earned runs over two IP with two strikeouts, one hit allowed, and zero walks.
Looking more broadly, since returning from the IL on September 18, Diaz has turned in seven scoreless innings with 11 strikeouts.
More MLB on Heavy: Kike Hernandez Making MLB History Shouldn’t Surprise Los Angeles Dodgers Fans
Quickly Taking a Look at Edwin Diaz’s Career with the Mets
Edwin Diaz was an All-Star with the New York Mets in 2022 and 2025.
Across 328.1 IP with the Mets, Diaz posted an ERA of 2.93 with 144 saves and 538 strikeouts.
When right (and healthy), Diaz is one of MLB’s most dominant relievers.
It was tough that the Mets had to let go of Edwin Diaz, who had been a staple of their relievers’ corps for several years, but New York was unable to match the Dodgers’ massive offer for the 32-year-old right-hander.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Must Demote Ronald Acuña Jr. Before NLDS Game 4

item.title: [Heavy.com] Kike Hernandez Making MLB History Shouldn't Surprise Los Angeles Dodgers Fans
item.dc:creator: TJ French
item.description: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 06: Enrique Hernández #8 of the Los Angeles Dodgers hits a two run home run during the fourth inning against the Atlanta Braves in game three of the National League Division Series at Truist Park on October 06, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) If you have been a Los Angeles Dodgers fan for the past X amount of years, you are aware that Kike Hernandez has been a playoff hero on several occasions. Well, in his first playoff at-bats this Octo
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 06: Enrique Hernández #8 of the Los Angeles Dodgers hits a two run home run during the fourth inning against the Atlanta Braves in game three of the National League Division Series at Truist Park on October 06, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images)
If you have been a Los Angeles Dodgers fan for the past X amount of years, you are aware that Kike Hernandez has been a playoff hero on several occasions.
Well, in his first playoff at-bats this October in Game Three of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves, Hernandez made his mark known once again with a huge 2-run home run off Chris Sale.
Hernandez’s October heroics feel inevitable at this point, and if the Dodgers are facing a left-handed starter going forward, Kike will almost certainly be in the lineup.
With his fourth-inning home run on Tuesday, Kike Hernandez made a unique piece of MLB history.
“Kiké Hernández is the only player in MLB history to have at least 10.0% of his career homers (reg & post) come in the postseason (min. 100 total homers).”
That is a pretty wild stat, and here are the official percentage numbers for Kike, as relayed by Opta:
Hernández is currently at 11.3% (17/151). The next-highest mark (min. 100 total homers) is 9.4% by Jose Altuve (28/299).
The legend of Kike Hernandez rolls along, and this piece of MLB history shouldn’t surprise any Dodgers fans, who have seen him do this over and over.
Kike Hernandez’s Name Will Be Etched in Dodgers History Forever
GettyLOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – SEPTEMBER 09: Enrique Hernández #8 of the Los Angeles Dodgers hits a two-run double against the Cincinnati Reds during the fourth inning of the MLB game at Dodger Stadium on September 09, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images)
Kike Hernandez has seen limited opportunities in the regular season over the past few seasons, but whenever his name is called upon in the MLB playoffs, he doesn’t miss his moment to shine.
It’s pretty remarkable what a playoff hitter he is, and his name has certainly been etched in Dodgers history for his improbable swings.
Under that post by OptaSTATS, there are a few reactions worth noting about Kike:
@The_Parent_Game: “Kiké Hernández spends 162 games making you forget he exists and then 30 seconds in October making you remember. The regular season is just his loading screen.”
@chloescoldnight: “kiké has been a playoff monster every single time he steps up and thats just facts. dodgers fans knew before the numbers did”
@smsportsguy: “Kike must be corking his bat or something. He’s a bum for 6 months every year and then becomes Mr. October.”
@allunsolicited: “Hernandez has 328 plate appearances in the playoffs which is just absurd. .486 slugging in the playoffs vs .402 regular season. One of the more remarkable baseball careers.”
TJ French covers the MLB for Heavy. TJ is a graduate of the University of Georgia. He has 2+ years of writing experience.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Dave Roberts shares Shohei Ohtani's reaction to being dropped in Dodgers lineup
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Abdón Ibarra
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts decided to drop Shohei Ohtani to fifth in the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Division Series amid the designated hitter’s ongoing struggles. Having a tough left-handed assignment on the mound in Chris Sale influenced Roberts’ decision, and Ohtani completely bought in. “Runs are going to be hard to come by. We all understand that,” Roberts began. “Sale’s going to b
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts decided to drop Shohei Ohtani to fifth in the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Division Series amid the designated hitter’s ongoing struggles.
Ohtani was 2-for-8 in the series entering play Tuesday against the Atlanta Braves. Having a tough left-handed assignment on the mound in Chris Sale influenced Roberts’ decision, and Ohtani completely bought in.
“Runs are going to be hard to come by. We all understand that,” Roberts began. “Sale’s going to be tough. But the guys I feel at the top have a good chance to get on base, and I do think that there’s going to be opportunities where the game, the situation, bleeds into Shohei’s at-bat.
“So I had a good conversation with him last night, told him my thoughts. And he completely understood and in all honesty, he said, ‘I was going to come to you in September and say, why don’t you hit me seventh?’ My point being, he wants to do whatever will help the team.
“So I feel good about this today. And it’s nothing as a sign of what’s more to come. It’s just for today specifically.”
The flow of the game played perfectly into the Dodgers’ strategy, as Ohtani was given prime RBI opportunities twice within the first three innings. But the results were not what Roberts had hoped for.
The Dodgers’ star struck out in the first inning to strand a runner in scoring position, but he did reach on catcher’s interference later in the third.
Because of the relationships Roberts has built with his players, he was not surprised Ohtani took the news well. While it was a difficult decision, Roberts felt it gave his team the best chance to counter Sale and the pitchers coming in after him.
“Not surprised at all. And I think that from day one, I’ve always said that my job is to do whatever is best for the team. And so I know I’ve built the equity and the trust in the players,” he said. “And so today I just feel this gives us the best chance to beat the Braves today and combat Sale, to combat what they’re going to throw after Sale. I feel good about it.”
The Dodgers’ skipper also hoped the change would help Ohtani stay within himself better than he has.
“I use that a lot, where it might give him a different look, let the game come to him a little bit later. I don’t think it’s a pressure thing. I do think it’s something where he wants to do more. But in that same breath, I do think that there’s going to be a couple big spots today where he’s going to be at-bat,” Roberts said.
Although Sale presents a wholly unique challenge for any left-handed hitter, Ohtani chased plenty out of the zone in the first inning. The Braves starter attacked the outside part of the plate and effectively tunneled his fastball and slider to get Ohtani to chase.
Ohtani worked a 3-0 count in his third at-bat against Sale but lost a challenge on what he thought was ball four and proceeded to get beaten by a fastball inside for a flyout.
Rather than signaling a lack of confidence, Roberts believes Ohtani nearly initiating the lineup change himself is an example of self-scouting.
“He’s a very good self-evaluator, a very high competitor and expects a lot from himself. I still think he’s very confident. But Sale’s a different monster. He’s tough, certainly, against lefties. But I still think he’s confident,” Roberts said.
“So now with that, just getting him back in the zone, and that’s easier said than done, I understand that. But there’s going to be high velocity trying to crowd him in to then spin him off. Is Shohei willing to take the knock to left field as he did against Dodd? So those are the things you’re looking for tonight.”
Shohei Ohtani’s lineup spot in Game 4
The Braves have right-hander Tyler Mahle on the mound to start against Tyler Glasnow in Game 4. However, Roberts said that does not necessarily guarantee that Ohtani will be back in the leadoff spot.
“Mahle is certainly a neutral, you could argue a reverse. So I don’t know that answer. Yes, he does throw with his right hand, but I haven’t made that decision quite yet,” he said.
Roberts did not specify if Ohtani’s at-bats on Thursday would tip the scale one way or the other, but the Dodgers’ skipper did confirm that the left-hander would not be batting in the fifth spot again.
If you love our reporting, choose DodgerBlue.com as a preferred source on Google.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Dodgers' Kiké Hernández Makes Incredible MLB History Thanks to Postseason Success
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Sandoval; Unknown
item.description: It's October, so of course Dodgers utility man Kiké Hernández is making an impact. On Tuesday, the Dodgers took back home-field advantage and secured a 2-1 series lead over the Atlanta Braves with their 3-1 win. They are one win away from their third consecutive National League Championship Series appearance and fifth in the last seven seasons. item.content:encoded:
It's October, so of course Dodgers utility man Kiké Hernández is making an impact.
On Tuesday, the Dodgers took back home-field advantage and secured a 2-1 series lead over the Atlanta Braves with their 3-1 win. They are one win away from their third consecutive National League Championship Series appearance and fifth in the last seven seasons.
Hernández's play once again helped the Dodgers to a victory in October, and in the process, he made MLB history.
According to OptaSTATS, Hernández is the only player in MLB history to have at least 10% of his career home runs (regular season and postseason) come in the postseason (minimum 100 total homers).
The 35-year-old is currently at 11.3% (17-out-of-151). OptaSTATS said that the next closest is Houston Astros' Jose Altuve at 9.4%.
The veteran Dodger transforms into a stud once the calendar flips to October. He goes from a steady utility player in the regular season into a postseason monster, boosting his career OPS from .706 up to .831.
“It’s something I take a lot of pride in, but don’t think about it too much,” Hernández said after the game. “Once I’m done playing, I’m going to be someone that looks back and be really proud of my career because of how my career has gone in terms of finding myself each and every year in October.”
Kiké Hernández Takes His Game to Another Level in October
In the past, the longtime Dodger has noted that the intensity and stakes of the postseason sharply elevate his focus and adrenaline compared to the grind of a 162-game regular season.
In 105 postseason games, the Puerto Rican native has hit .272 with a .831 OPS, 17 home runs, 44 RBIs and 81 hits in 298 at-bats.
The Dodgers have scored 10 runs through three games in the NLDS, all of which have come via the long ball. That is the longest streak to start a postseason in MLB history.
Hernández's home run in the fourth inning broke a scoreless tie. It was a two-run shot to left field with Andy Pages on base.
"He's a big-time player," manager Dave Roberts said after the game. "I said earlier, we needed a little bit of that Kiké dust. And he's always prepared. And he loves moments like this. He has a way to lock in. ... It's just one of those things that having him in a lineup in the postseason just adds that extra sort of urgency, that kind of grit that you need."
Two batters later, Freddie Freeman hit a solo shot to right-center against his former team to extend the lead to 3-0.
That was more then enough for ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was on it on Tuesday night.
The 28-year-old pitched seven great innings, allowing just one run on four hits with 10 strikeouts across 98 pitches.
Yamamoto is 33-0 (including the postseason) when he gets at least three runs of support.
The Dodgers will look to close out the series on Wednesday, with first pitch is at 3 p.m. PT.

Ricardo Sandoval is a freelance writer with On SI. He is a graduate of California State University, Northridge, and specializes in sports writing, particularly in MLB, NBA and NFL. He previously served as an Associate Editor for Dodgers Nation and has worked with Newsweek and The Sporting News.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Kiké Hernandez Proves Once Again He’s Built for Dodgers Postseason Moments
item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers veteran Kiké Hernández, in yet another stroke of postseason magic, delivered when the team needed him the most. Kike Hernandez’s moment After the Dodgers struggled offensively in Game 2, and with a lefty on the mound — an all-world pitcher nonetheless, like Chris Sale — manager Dave Roberts turned to Hernandez to start in Game 3 of the NLDS. Despite not featuring much during the regular season and producing little when he did, Hernandez hit a two-run home run against Sale. It
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers veteran Kiké Hernández, in yet another stroke of postseason magic, delivered when the team needed him the most.
Kike Hernandez’s moment
After the Dodgers struggled offensively in Game 2, and with a lefty on the mound — an all-world pitcher nonetheless, like Chris Sale — manager Dave Roberts turned to Hernandez to start in Game 3 of the NLDS.
Despite not featuring much during the regular season and producing little when he did, Hernandez hit a two-run home run against Sale.
It opened the scoring for the Dodgers and gave Yoshinobu Yamamoto a cushion. Those two runs would have been enough, with Freddie Freeman’s solo shot serving as insurance.
For Hernandez to deliver once again, now 35 years old, it really does show that there is something about high-stakes moments that bring out the best in Hernandez.
“He’s a big-time player,” Roberts said. “We needed a little bit of that Kiké dust. He’s always prepared and he loves moments like this. … Having him in the lineup in the postseason just adds that extra sort of urgency, that kind of grit that you need.”
How Kike Hernandez always delivers in the postseason
Freeman, who has seen and done a lot in baseball, celebrated how ready Hernandez stays for these kinds of moments.
“I wish there was a recipe for that so we can all take it from him,” Freeman said.
“He’s incredible. He shows up when you need him. He hasn’t had a start in a while, and he goes out there and does what he did. … He’s a Swiss Army knife, and he’s ready to go at all times.”
Hernandez’s home run was the 17th of his postseason career. In fact, he is now the only player in MLB history to have at least 10.0% of his career homers come in the postseason, with at least 100 career home runs.
“That’s probably something that, once I’m done playing, I’m going to look back and be really proud of my career because of how I find myself each and every year in October,” he said.
Until he is done, the Dodgers may need to count on Hernandez one more time, and he will keep himself ready.

With Game 3 of the National League Division Series scoreless in the top of the fourth inning and a runner on first base with nobody out, Hernández crushed a changeup from Atlanta Braves ace Chris Sale over the left field wall for a two-run home run, giving the Dodgers a 2-0 lead. Ultimately, that long
item.content:encoded:
Dodgers Manager Dave Roberts Raves About 'Big-Time Player' Kiké Hernández
Kiké Hernández only has one hit in the 2026 MLB playoffs, but it's the biggest hit of the year for the Los Angeles Dodgers.
With Game 3 of the National League Division Series scoreless in the top of the fourth inning and a runner on first base with nobody out, Hernández crushed a changeup from Atlanta Braves ace Chris Sale over the left field wall for a two-run home run, giving the Dodgers a 2-0 lead. Ultimately, that long ball would be enough for Los Angeles to get a 3-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves and take a 2-1 series lead.
"He's a big-time player," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said of Hernández in his postgame press conference on Tuesday night. "I said it earlier, we needed a little bit of that Kiké dust, and he's always prepared, and he loves moments like this. He has a way to lock in. He doubled up on a changeup, and he put a good swing on it and made a couple really nice defensive plays, as well.
"It's just one of those things where having him in a lineup in the postseason just adds that extra sort of urgency and that kind of grit that you need."
The aforementioned home run was the 12th postseason long ball for Hernández in a Dodgers uniform; Hernández, who has extensive experience at every position but catcher (he has even made 11 appearances on the mound), is in his second stint and 10th overall season with the Dodgers (2015-20 and 2023-present).
Two batters after Hernández went deep, first baseman Freddie Freeman did the same, launching a solo home run to right. On the hill, Los Angeles got seven potent innings from right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who logged 10 strikeouts and gave up just one run and five baserunners (four hits and one walk). Tanner Scott and Edwin Díaz followed with a scoreless inning of relief apiece.
The 35-year-old Hernández, who traditionally gets lauded for his defensive play and versatility, has been a postseason hero for the Dodgers. With Los Angeles trailing the Toronto Blue Jays 3-2 in the 2025 World Series and trying to extend the series, Hernández turned a game-ending double-play in left field with the tying run in scoring position to force Game 7, which the Dodgers would win in 11 innings.
In 2020, Hernández hit a game-tying home run in the bottom of the sixth inning against the Braves in Game 7 of the NLCS, which the Dodgers went on to win, and he drove in one of the Dodgers' two runs against the San Diego Padres in Game 5 of the 2024 NLDS on a solo home run.
Meanwhile, Hernández blasted three home runs for the Dodgers in a closeout Game 5 victory over the Chicago Cubs in the 2017 NLCS and hit five home runs across 11 postseason games for the Boston Red Sox in 2021.
Hernández, who started at third base for the Dodgers in Game 3 and later moved to left field, was limited to 41 games in the 2026 regular season due to elbow and oblique injuries, respectively.
In all, the Dodgers have scored just 10 runs in the NLDS, but they've held the Braves to seven runs. The Dodgers have the chance to advance to the NL Championship Series in Game 4 on Wednesday afternoon (6 p.m. ET on FS1). Atlanta will send Tyler Mahle to the hill, while Los Angeles counters with Tyler Glasnow.
Should the Dodgers advance, they'd play the winner of the NLDS matchup between the Milwaukee Brewers and Padres, who staved off elimination with a Game 3 win on Tuesday night, in the NLCS.

item.title: [El Nuevo Día] ¡Boricuas brillan en octubre! Kike Hernández jonronea y Edwin Díaz salva juego en Atlanta
item.dc:creator: Charles Odum
item.description: 7 de octubre de 2026 - 9:45 PM Atlanta - Yoshinobu Yamamoto ponchó a 10 bateadores en siete entradas, Enrique “Kike” Hernández conectó un jonrón de dos carreras y los Dodgers de Los Ángeles vencieron 3-1 a los Braves de Atlanta el martes por la noche, tomando una ventaja de 2-1 en su Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional. item.content:encoded:
7 de octubre de 2026 - 9:45 PM
Atlanta - Yoshinobu Yamamoto ponchó a 10 bateadores en siete entradas, Enrique “Kike” Hernández conectó un jonrón de dos carreras y los Dodgers de Los Ángeles vencieron 3-1 a los Braves de Atlanta el martes por la noche, tomando una ventaja de 2-1 en su Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional.
Hernández, quien suele brillar en octubre, sacudió su decimoséptimo cuadrangular en postemporada, quebrando un empate con el miembro del Salón de la Fama de Béisbol Carlos Beltrán.
El boricua ahora está empate con Jim Thome, Aaron Judge y David Ortiz en la lista de jonrones en la postemporada.
Yamamoto dominó el muy esperado duelo contra el as de Atlanta, Chris Sale, quien permitió tres carreras y siete imparables en cinco entradas. Yamamoto, Jugador Más Valioso (MVP) de la Serie Mundial de 2025, concedió solo cuatro hits y una base por bolas, mejorando su récord de postemporada a 8-1.
Los Dodgers pueden ganar la serie —pactada al mejor de cinco juegos— y dar un paso más en su intento de convertirse en el primer equipo de la Liga Nacional en ganar tres títulos consecutivos de Serie Mundial si vencen nuevamente a los Braves el miércoles por la noche en el cuarto partido.
Los Braves esperaban que dar descanso adicional a Sale fuera una fórmula ganadora para este crucial tercer encuentro. Sin embargo, tras dejar a seis corredores en base en las primeras tres entradas, permitió el jonrón de dos carreras de Hernández y un cuadrangular solitario de Freddie Freeman en el cuarto episodio.
Ozzie Albies abrió la novena entrada de Atlanta con un doblete contra el muro entre el jardín derecho y el central ante los lanzamientos de Edwin Díaz, avanzando a tercera base tras un rodado de out de Michael Harris II. Díaz dejó al corredor varado cuando Mauricio Dubón fue puesto out en un elevado de foul al jardín derecho y Mike Yastrzemski fue retirado con un rodado al campocorto Mookie Betts.
Tras una temporada agobiado por lesiones, Díaz se apuntó su primer salvado desde el pasado 14 de agosto, cuando lanzó la novena entrada en blanco contra Milwaukee.
FUe además su primer rescate de postemporada desde el 14 de octubre de 2024, cuanto se apuntó un salvamento por los Mets de Nueva York contra los propios Dodgers en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional.
Dubón realizó una atrapada saltando sobre la barda del jardín izquierdo para robarle un jonrón a Freeman en la tercera entrada; sin embargo, Freeman logró conectar su cuadrangular una entrada más tarde. El jonrón de Hernández hacia el jardín izquierdo impulsó a Andy Pages, quien había conectado un sencillo. Un out después, Freeman conectó el jonrón número 18 de su carrera en postemporada hacia el jardín derecho, ampliando la ventaja a 3-0.
El mánager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, bajó al bateador designado Shohei Ohtani al quinto puesto del orden al bate, debido a que Ohtani registraba un promedio de 3 de 15 en su carrera contra Sale. Ohtani se había ido de 4-0 con dos ponches ante Sale cuando los Dodgers perdieron 1-0 el 26 de agosto en Atlanta. Roberts predijo acertadamente que Ohtani tendría oportunidades con corredores en base al batear en una posición más baja del orden de bateo.
En la primera entrada, con corredores en primera y segunda, Sale ponchó a Ohtani para cerrar el episodio. En la tercera, con dos corredores en base, Ohtani llegó a primera gracias a una interferencia del receptor Drake Baldwin —lo que llenó las bases—, antes de que Miguel Rojas terminara la entrada con un elevado al jardín derecho. Ohtani recibió una base por bolas al abrir la octava entrada frente a Brent Suter, el cuarto lanzador de Atlanta.
Un rodado de Baldwin a primera base, con las bases llenas, impulsó a Dubón —quien había conectado un sencillo— en la quinta entrada, anotando así la única carrera de Atlanta ante Yamamoto.
Rojas abandonó el partido durante un turno al bate en la octava entrada. El segunda base pareció lastimarse la espalda al realizar un swing y fue sustituido por Tommy Edman. Los Dodgers informaron que la lesión consistía en dolor en la zona lumbar.
Tanner Scott sumó dos ponches en una octava entrada sin anotaciones para Los Ángeles.
Las noticias explicadas de forma sencilla y directa para entender lo más importante del día.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers SP Yoshinobu Yamamoto Makes MLB History in NLDS Win
item.dc:creator: Jarrett Prendergrast
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are one win away from reaching the National League Championship Series for the third consecutive year. The Dodgers entered Game 3 of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves needing a crucial win to take a 2-1 series lead. That is why they called on Yoshinobu Yamamoto to start the game. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are one win away from reaching the National League Championship Series for the third consecutive year.
The Dodgers entered Game 3 of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves needing a crucial win to take a 2-1 series lead. That is why they called on Yoshinobu Yamamoto to start the game. Yamamoto has been a big-game pitcher throughout his career, and he won the World Series MVP last season.
The Dodgers started Yamamoto on the road for Game 3 against the Braves' ace Chris Sale. Yamamoto got the better of that matchup, throwing 7.0 innings, allowing only four hits and one run, and striking out 10.
The righty earned his first postseason win and set an historic record. According to OptaSTATS, Yamamoto is the only pitcher in MLB history to earn a win in five straight postseason appearances without allowing more than one run or one walk. Each of those wins has been on the road.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto is the only pitcher in MLB history to earn the win in 5 straight postseason appearances while not allowing more than 1 run or 1 walk in any of them.
All 5 have come on the road. https://t.co/QwWmubt7fS
— OptaSTATS (@OptaSTATS) October 7, 2026
It is hard to find a more dominant postseason pitcher in baseball than Yamamoto. He has been rock solid for a Dodgers pitching staff that has been often injured over the years.
Yamamoto's Postseason Prowess
What Yamamoto did last season is hard to replicate. In the 2025 World Series, Yamamoto threw 17.2 innings, allowed only 10 hits and two runs, and won three games, including Games 6 and 7.
His first playoff start this season picked up right where he left off. He will likely be a workhorse for the Dodgers again this postseason as they go for the elusive three-peat, which has only been done a few times in sports.
The next time we will likely see Yamamoto is in the NLCS if the Dodgers make it. However, if their season comes down to a Game 5 in the NLDS, we know Yamamoto will be available.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Dodgers SP Yoshinobu Yamamoto Makes MLB History in NLDS Win appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [WSLS] Yamamoto is dominant again as Dodgers ride homers from Hernández and Freeman to 3-1 win over Braves
item.dc:creator: Charles Odum; Associated Press
item.description: ATLANTA – Yoshinobu Yamamoto felt trust from Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts when he remained in a crucial NL Division Series game after a stressful fifth inning. “I’d like to continue living up to the highest expectation,” Yamamoto said through a translator. Recommended Videos The right-hander from Japan continues to do more than just meet expectations in the postseason. Yamamoto struck out 10 in seven brilliant innings, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run homer and the Dodgers beat the Atlan
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA – Yoshinobu Yamamoto felt trust from Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts when he remained in a crucial NL Division Series game after a stressful fifth inning.
“I’d like to continue living up to the highest expectation,” Yamamoto said through a translator.
Recommended Videos
The right-hander from Japan continues to do more than just meet expectations in the postseason.
Yamamoto struck out 10 in seven brilliant innings, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run homer and the Dodgers beat the Atlanta Braves 3-1 on Tuesday night to take a 2-1 lead in their NL Division Series.
Yamamoto dominated his much-anticipated matchup with Atlanta ace Chris Sale, who allowed three runs and seven hits in five innings. Last year's World Series MVP permitted only four hits and one walk while improving to 8-1 with a 2.14 ERA in 11 career postseason outings, including 10 starts.
His 10 strikeouts were a postseason high for him.
“I was confident and able to control all my pitches today,” Yamamoto said.
The Dodgers can clinch the best-of-five series and take another step toward becoming the first National League team to win three consecutive World Series by beating the Braves again Wednesday night in Game 4.
Atlanta hoped giving Sale extra rest would be a winning formula in the pivotal third game. Instead, after stranding six runners in the first three innings, he gave up the two-run homer to Hernández and a solo shot to former Braves star Freddie Freeman in the fourth.
“He was still touching 100 (mph),” manager Walt Weiss said of Sale. “The stuff was fine. Like I said, maybe the command not perfect. It wasn’t bad. But they did a nice job against him.”
That was all the offensive support Yamamoto and relievers Tanner Scott and Edwin Díaz would need.
Ozzie Albies opened the Atlanta ninth with a double off the right-center wall against Díaz and moved to third on Michael Harris II's groundout. Díaz stranded the runner and earned a save when Mauricio Dubón fouled out to right field and Mike Yastrzemski grounded out to shortstop Mookie Betts.
A homer for the boo birds
Freeman said he didn't mind being booed by Atlanta fans in the sellout crowd of 42,420.
“I’ve got a gray uniform on,” Freeman said. “I expect boos. It’s OK. ... It’s all love. I still love everybody here and I’m looking forward to tomorrow.”
Dubón made a leaping catch over the left-field wall to rob Freeman of a home run in the third. Freeman wouldn't be denied an inning later. Hernández's homer to left drove in Andy Pages, who singled. One out later, Freeman pulled his 18th career postseason homer to right field for a 3-0 lead.
Lineup change
Roberts moved designated hitter Shohei Ohtani down to No. 5 in the lineup because Ohtani was 3 for 15 in his career against Sale. Ohtani went 0 for 4 with two strikeouts against Sale when the Dodgers lost 1-0 on Aug. 26 in Atlanta.
Roberts correctly predicted Ohtani would have opportunities with runners on base hitting lower in the order.
With runners on first and second in the first, Sale struck out Ohtani to end the inning. With two runners on base in the third, Ohtani reached on catcher's interference by Drake Baldwin to load the bases before Miguel Rojas ended the inning with a flyball to right field. Ohtani walked to lead off the eighth against Brent Suter, Atlanta's fourth pitcher.
Baldwin's bases-loaded grounder to first base drove in Dubón, who singled, in the fifth for Atlanta's only run.
Injury report
Rojas left during an at-bat in the eighth. The second baseman appeared to injure his back on a swing and was replaced by Tommy Edman. The Dodgers announced the injury as lower back pain.
Roberts said Rojas probably won't start on Wednesday and his availability off the bench will be determined before the game.
“I give him credit for conceding that at-bat,” Roberts said.
Weiss made a late change, moving Ronald Acuña Jr. from right field to designated hitter. Weiss said Acuña jammed his knee on a slide in Game 2. Acuña remained in the game but the knee was sore on Tuesday, leading to the lineup change.
Milestone win for Roberts
Roberts now has 71 career postseason wins, tying Tony La Russa for second-most in major league history. Joe Torre is first with 84.
Up next
Braves right-hander Tyler Mahle is expected to face Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow in Game 4 on Wednesday night. Mahle said Tuesday an abdominal pull is now a “non-issue.” He felt the pull before allowing one run in seven innings of a 4-3 loss to Philadelphia in 10 innings during the NL Wild Card Series last week.
___

item.title: [MLB.com] Dubón le niega un jonrón a Freeman... pero Freddie cobra revancha después
item.dc:creator: Paul Casella
item.description: Después de que Sale consiguiera cada uno de sus primeros seis outs por la vía del ponche en el Juego 3 de la SDLN contra los Dodgers, Dubón registró el primer out defensivo y lo hizo de manera espectacular. Con un corredor en primera y nadie fuera en la parte alta del tercer inning, la exsuperestrella de los Bravos Freddie Freeman conectó un batazo profundo hacia el jardín izquierdo que salió de su bate a 101.3 mph. Dubón siguió la trayectoria de la pelota hasta la pared y calculó perfectamente
item.content:encoded:
Después de que Sale consiguiera cada uno de sus primeros seis outs por la vía del ponche en el Juego 3 de la SDLN contra los Dodgers, Dubón registró el primer out defensivo y lo hizo de manera espectacular.
Con un corredor en primera y nadie fuera en la parte alta del tercer inning, la exsuperestrella de los Bravos Freddie Freeman conectó un batazo profundo hacia el jardín izquierdo que salió de su bate a 101.3 mph. Dubón siguió la trayectoria de la pelota hasta la pared y calculó perfectamente su salto para realizar la atrapada justo frente a un grupo de relevistas de los Dodgers, quienes se preparaban para que la bola cayera en el bullpen de los visitantes.
La atrapada de Dubón probablemente le robó un posible jonrón de dos carreras a Freeman, pero como mínimo evitó un extrabase y, casi con toda seguridad, una carrera o dos en el episodio.
Los Dodgers llenaron las bases gracias a un sencillo de Will Smith con dos outs y a que Shohei Ohtani llegó a salvo por interferencia del receptor, pero Sale salió ileso al hacer que Miguel Rojas conectara una línea al jardín derecho para terminar la entrada.
Antes de siquiera necesitar la ayuda de su defensa, Sale se unió a Mike Hampton (Juego 2 de la SDLN del 2003) como los únicos lanzadores de los Bravos en conseguir cada uno de sus primeros seis outs por la vía del ponche en un juego de postemporada.
Freeman se desquitó en su siguiente turno al bate, cuando disparó con autoridad un cuadrangular hacia el jardín derecho-central, el 18vo vuelacercas de su carrera en postemporada, para darle a los Dodgers una ventaja de 3-0.
